reports.howItWorks: Victims receive a call, voicemail, or text — often from someone identifying himself as "Dan" — claiming government records show a specific dollar amount (commonly cited around $5,286) is waiting for them in a relief check tied to "past relief programs or federal assistance payments." The message urges the victim to visit a website such as myreliefcheck.com or myreliefclaim.com to search their name and "collect it before it's returned." The site is not affiliated with any real government agency; instead, it prompts victims to enter personal identifying information and banking details to "claim" the payment. Handing over this data exposes victims to identity theft, drained bank accounts, and continued follow-up contact from scammers via additional calls, texts, or emails attempting to extract more money or information. The scam has been amplified by news coverage of the recent federal government shutdown, which scammers exploit to make the "relief payment" premise feel more plausible.
redFlags: Unsolicited call, voicemail, or text claiming you have an unclaimed government relief check waiting
You're told to visit a third-party website (not a .gov domain) and "search your name" to claim money
A vague personal name like "Dan" is used with no verifiable agency affiliation
Urgency pressure to act "before it's returned"
Requests for personal identifying information or bank details to "release" a payment
Ties the offer to current news events like a government shutdown or old COVID-era relief programs
realExamples: BBB Scam Tracker received over 900 reports nationally about the myreliefcheck.com/myreliefclaim.com scheme, with victims reporting calls, voicemails, and texts from a caller identifying himself as "Dan" claiming a specific dollar amount was waiting for them
Local BBB chapters in Michigan and North Alabama reported the scam spreading to their regions within the past two months, with over 800 reports logged during that period
Victims reported the scam intensifying alongside news coverage of the federal government shutdown, with fraudsters exploiting shutdown-related anxiety about federal payments
reports.source: Better Business Bureau, "BBB Scam Alert: Fake relief check phone calls claim you have money waiting" - https://www.bbb.org/all/consumer/scam/fake-relief-check-scam

reports.title: Gold Bar & Bulk Cash Courier Scam
reports.summary: Scammers impersonating grandchildren, government agents, or tech support convince mostly elderly victims to withdraw cash or buy gold bars, then send an in-person courier to physically collect the loot from the victim's home.
relatedScams: FTC Official Impersonation Bitcoin ATM Scam
FTC Impersonator Fake Employee ID Refund Recovery Scam
safetyTips: Never give cash, gold, or valuables to a courier sent by someone who contacted you unsolicited by phone, email, or pop-up
Independently verify any claim of a relative's emergency or government/legal trouble by calling them or the agency directly using a number you look up yourself
Real government agencies (FBI, IRS, Social Security, etc.) will never ask you to buy gold bars or hand cash to a courier
Talk to a trusted family member or your bank before withdrawing large sums or buying precious metals under pressure
Report suspected courier pickup scams to the FBI's IC3.gov and local police immediately, even if you're embarrassed
reports.howItWorks: A fraudster first gains a victim's trust through a grandparent-emergency call, a government/law-enforcement impersonation call, or a tech-support pop-up, convincing the victim their money is at risk or a relative is in trouble. Instead of asking for a wire transfer or gift cards, the scammer instructs the victim to withdraw large amounts of cash or, increasingly, to purchase physical gold bars from a dealer "to protect the funds." The criminal then arranges for a courier, sometimes an unwitting rideshare driver and sometimes a knowing accomplice, to come to the victim's home or a nearby meeting point to physically pick up the cash or gold. To make the handoff seem legitimate, the scammer often gives the victim a verification "code," "password," or "serial number" that the courier must recite before the victim hands over the money or gold.
redFlags: A caller you don't know instructs you to withdraw cash or buy gold bars and hand them to a stranger who comes to your door
You're told to give a courier a special code, password, or serial number to verify who should receive the money
Urgent claims that a family member is in legal trouble, your accounts are compromised, or the government needs you to move your money to "protect" it
Instructions to keep the transaction secret from other family members or bank staff
Pressure to act immediately with no time to verify the story independently
realExamples: FBI Boston documented 103 gold bar and bulk cash courier scam cases across New England from 2023 to May 2025, with losses totaling over $26 million, about 98% involving victims over age 60.
Nationwide, the FBI documented at least 1,737 instances of courier pickups of bulk cash or gold bars during the same period, with losses of roughly $186 million.
A South Boston man was indicted for allegedly defrauding a 75-year-old man in Berkshire County out of $500,000 through this scheme.
reports.source: FBI Boston Division, "FBI Boston Warns of Increase in Gold Bar and Bulk Cash Courier Scams," September 22, 2025, https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/boston/news/fbi-boston-warns-of-increase-in-gold-bar-and-bulk-cash-courier-scams

reports.title: Deepfake Job Candidate / Fake AI Employee Scam
reports.summary: Scammers, many linked to North Korean state-sponsored operations, use AI deepfake video/audio, stolen identities, and ChatGPT-polished resumes to get hired into remote jobs, then use the position to steal company data, plant malware, or funnel salary payments overseas.
safetyTips: Verify identity documents in person or via a live, unscripted video check where you ask the candidate to turn their head to the side or perform an unscripted action a deepfake would struggle to replicate
Cross-check the shipping address for company equipment against the candidate's stated home address and reject freight-forwarding or unfamiliar third-party addresses
Use identity-verification and deepfake-detection tools during high-stakes remote hiring for sensitive IT or data-access roles
Limit new remote hires' system access and monitor for anomalous VPN logins, unusual work hours, or connections from unexpected countries during onboarding
Train HR and hiring managers to recognize red flags of AI-generated resumes, synthetic photos, and coached video interviews, and report suspected cases to the FBI/IC3
reports.howItWorks: A fraudster builds a fake professional identity using a stolen or synthetic Social Security number, an AI-generated or "face-swapped" profile photo, and an AI-polished resume, then applies for legitimate remote tech or IT jobs. During video interviews, the applicant uses real-time deepfake face-swap and voice-cloning software (sometimes with a live "coach" typing answers) to appear as a different, more qualified or more "American-sounding" person than they really are. Once hired, the fake employee (in many documented cases tied to North Korean IT worker schemes) receives a company laptop, often routed to a US-based "laptop farm," logs in via VPN, and either collects a legitimate salary that gets funneled overseas to fund weapons programs, or uses insider access to exfiltrate sensitive data, install malware, or extort the employer after termination. Security researchers report the fraud has scaled dramatically, with some hiring managers estimating a huge share of remote-job applicants are now fake AI-generated candidates.
redFlags: Candidate's lip movements, blinking, or facial edges look slightly out of sync or glitchy during video calls, especially at profile angles or with rapid head movement
Applicant refuses to turn on camera for parts of the interview or gives excuses for poor video/audio quality
Resume, LinkedIn history, and interview answers feel AI-polished but generic, or the candidate's home address, bank routing details, and shipping address for equipment don't match
Candidate insists on having a company laptop shipped to an address that turns out to be a freight-forwarding or 'laptop farm' location rather than their stated home
Multiple candidates for different job postings share similar resume phrasing, photos, or reference contacts
New hire immediately requests VPN access, remote log-in tools, or asks to reroute the equipment shortly after onboarding
realExamples: Cybersecurity training firm KnowBe4 disclosed in July 2024 that it unknowingly hired a North Korean IT worker who used a stolen US identity and an AI-enhanced photo to pass background checks and interviews, and was caught only after malware activity was flagged on his first day.

Voice-security firm Pindrop's CEO described catching a fake remote-job candidate dubbed "Ivan X" who used deepfake software and generative AI tools during interviews to try to get hired at the company.

The FBI and IC3 have issued multiple advisories since 2022 warning businesses about North Korean IT workers using witting and unwitting US-based facilitators, fraudulent documents, and now increasingly deepfake technology to secure remote technical jobs at US companies.
reports.source: FBI/IC3 Advisory "North Korean IT Workers Conducting Data Extortion" (ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250123); NYSBA "Addressing the Threat of Fake Job Candidates" (nysba.org, May 2026); CNBC "Fake job seekers use AI to interview for remote jobs" (April 8, 2025)

reports.title: AI-Cloned Fake Vehicle Dealership Scam
reports.summary: Scammers use AI tools to clone real dealership websites or build entirely fake auto/RV dealership sites and Facebook ad campaigns, then convince buyers to wire large sums for vehicles that don't exist.
relatedScams: Fake Heavy Equipment & Vehicle Dealer Website Scam
Fake Vehicle History Report Scam for Car Sellers
safetyTips: Independently look up the dealership's phone number and address rather than using contact info from the ad or website, and call to verify the vehicle and transaction directly
Visit the dealership in person or verify its physical existence via Google Street View before wiring any funds
Never wire money for a vehicle sight-unseen; use verifiable, traceable payment methods and complete the purchase at a legitimate, confirmed dealership location
Reverse-image-search listing photos to check if they've been copied or AI-altered from another source
Be suspicious of deals advertised primarily through social media ads offering prices well below market value
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters build convincing dealership websites using AI-generated or AI-altered photos, sometimes cloning an existing legitimate dealer's name, staff listings, and inventory, or inventing a fake company entirely. They advertise heavily on Facebook and other social platforms, often listing a real-looking business address that turns out to be an empty lot or unrelated location. When a buyer inquires, scammers engage in days- or weeks-long conversations to build trust and answer questions convincingly before pressuring the victim to wire money for a vehicle that was never actually for sale, at which point communication stops and the money is gone. Risk-management researchers have identified over a hundred of these "dealership cloning" sites impersonating active or defunct dealers.
redFlags: Dealership's website photos look slightly off, too polished, or have inconsistent details when zoomed in (AI-altered images)
Seller insists on a wire transfer before you can see the vehicle in person or meet at the dealership
Listed business address turns out to be a parking lot, empty building, or unrelated business when checked on Google Maps
Misspelled business name or slight variations from a real, known dealership name
Heavy pressure to move quickly on a 'too good to be true' price advertised via a Facebook or social media ad
Communication happens only by text/chat/email with no way to verify a real, listed phone number
realExamples: A North Carolina buyer wired $77,300 for a Lexus GX 550 after scammers cloned a real dealership's online identity; the vehicle and transaction were entirely fraudulent and the real dealership had no involvement.

The BBB warned about a fake RV dealership, listed as Accelerated Motors LLC, that advertised on Facebook with a Baton Rouge address that was actually an empty parking lot with no RVs, using AI-altered photos and a misspelled business name.
Risk management firm Point Predictive identified more than 100 'dealership cloning' websites impersonating active or defunct dealerships nationwide.
reports.source: Auto Finance News, autofinancenews.net/allposts/risk-management/ai-cloning-scam-impersonates-dealerships-with-fake-websites/; Autoblog, autoblog.com/news/ai-is-making-fake-car-dealerships-look-real-and-its-costing-buyers-thousands; WAFB, wafb.com/2026/07/22/bbb-warns-ai-powered-rv-dealer-scam-targeting-facebook-users/

reports.title: Spoofed IC3/FBI Fraud-Reporting Website Scam
reports.summary: Criminals are building near-exact clones of the FBI's official Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3.gov) website to steal personal and financial data from people who are trying to report a scam they were already victimized by.
safetyTips: Type www.ic3.gov directly into your browser's address bar instead of searching for it, and never click 'sponsored' search results
Double-check that the URL ends in .gov and reads exactly www.ic3.gov before entering any information
Never send money or provide banking passwords to anyone contacting you about a complaint you filed or offering to recover lost funds
If you suspect you used a spoofed site, monitor your accounts, place a fraud alert with credit bureaus, and file a genuine report directly on ic3.gov
reports.howItWorks: Scam victims searching online for how to report fraud, or who click a "sponsored" search ad, social media post, or link shared in a scam-recovery group, land on a fake site built to look like the real IC3.gov complaint portal, often using a domain with slight misspellings or a different top-level domain. The cloned page mimics the FBI seal, banner text, and even the genuine site's own warning about impersonators, then presents a "complaint form" that harvests names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, and banking details. Some versions follow up by emailing a fake confirmation of the "report," or by having a scammer posing as IC3/FBI personnel contact the victim on messaging apps to offer fund "recovery," pushing them toward a second round of financial loss.
redFlags: Arriving at 'ic3' or 'FBI' report sites through a search ad, social media post, or a link someone else sent rather than typing the address yourself
URL that is close to but not exactly www.ic3.gov (extra words, hyphens, or a non-.gov ending)
Being contacted afterward by someone claiming to be FBI/IC3 staff offering to help recover money you reported losing
Low-quality graphics, odd phrasing, or a complaint form asking for banking log-in details or payment before it will 'process' your report
realExamples: The FBI's IC3 identified the first wave of these fraudulent sites on September 18, 2025, after visitors reported receiving deceptive emails confirming fake IC3 report submissions.
Security researchers found cloned pages reproducing the FBI seal, IC3 banner, and complaint form, making them nearly indistinguishable from the authentic site.
Reported instances describe cybercrime groups using Facebook and search-engine ads to spread the phishing sites and drive traffic to them.
reports.source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, PSA "Threat Actors Spoofing the FBI IC3 Website for Possible Malicious Activity," https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250919

reports.title: "Ghost Tapping" Contactless Payment Scam
reports.summary: Scammers exploit NFC "tap-to-pay" technology to charge victims' cards or phones without authorization, often by posing as vendors or charity collectors at crowded markets, fairs, and festivals.
relatedScams: Brushing Scam with QR Code Twist
safetyTips: Keep cards and NFC-enabled phones in an RFID-blocking wallet or sleeve when not actively paying
Always glance at the terminal screen to confirm the merchant name and exact amount before tapping
Set up real-time transaction alerts with your bank or card issuer so you're notified of every charge immediately
Avoid storing more cards than necessary in mobile wallet apps to limit exposure if a device is compromised
Regularly review bank and card statements for small, unrecognized charges, especially after crowded public events
Verify charity collectors' identification and prefer donating directly through an organization's official website instead of an in-person tap-to-pay request
reports.howItWorks: "Ghost tapping" abuses Near Field Communication (NFC), the wireless technology that lets contactless cards and mobile wallets exchange payment data at very close range. In one version, a fraudster poses as a market vendor, food stall, or charity fundraiser who only accepts tap-to-pay, approaches the victim closely, and uses an altered or portable card reader to charge far more than the agreed amount while rushing the victim so they don't check the terminal screen or get a receipt. In another version, criminals use a hidden RFID/NFC reader to "bump" or get within a couple of inches of an unprotected card or phone in a crowd (subway, concert, festival) and skim payment credentials, sometimes loading them into a relay app on another phone to make fraudulent purchases elsewhere. Victims often don't notice anything happened until small, repeated unauthorized charges appear on their statements later.
redFlags: A vendor, fundraiser, or seller who insists on tap-to-pay only and refuses cash or chip/PIN alternatives
The person rushes you through the transaction, blocks your view of the card reader screen, or doesn't give you a receipt
Someone stands unusually close to you or bumps into you in a crowded place like a fair, festival, or public transit
Small, unfamiliar charges appear on your card or digital wallet statement after visiting a crowded event
A door-to-door 'charity' collector asks for tap-to-pay donations without proper identification or paperwork
realExamples: BBB Scam Tracker received a report of an individual going door-to-door claiming to collect charity donations who accepted only tap-to-pay and charged victims' accounts amounts ranging from roughly $537 to $1,100 without authorization.
Consumers reported scammers posing as vendors at markets, pop-ups, or craft fairs who used altered card terminals to overcharge tap-to-pay customers while rushing them and withholding receipts.

Security researchers have tracked a rise in 'Ghost Tap' Android malware that relays stolen NFC/tap-to-pay credentials to cash-out networks, with hundreds of thousands of dollars in fraudulent transactions linked to illicitly obtained POS terminals advertised on Telegram.
reports.source: Better Business Bureau / Fox News, "How to protect yourself from ghost-tapping payment card scams nationwide," https://www.foxnews.com/tech/ghost-tapping-scam-targets-tap-to-pay-users

reports.title: Fake VPN App Malware Scam
reports.summary: Cybercriminals are distributing malicious apps and browser extensions disguised as popular VPN services to secretly install info-stealing and banking malware on victims' devices.
safetyTips: Only download VPN apps from official app stores and the provider's verified official domain, double-checking for misspellings
Avoid free VPN services that request permissions unrelated to VPN functionality, like access to contacts or messages
Research the VPN provider's reputation and reviews before installing, and prefer well-established, paid providers with transparent privacy policies
Enable enhanced protection features (e.g., Chrome's Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection) that warn against malicious sites and fraudulent downloads
Remember a VPN masks your IP address but does not guarantee total anonymity or safety—treat any app claiming otherwise with skepticism
reports.howItWorks: Scammers build convincing lookalike VPN apps or browser extensions that impersonate well-known, trusted VPN brands, then distribute them through official app stores, ads, and other platforms using misleading marketing, sexually suggestive ads, or trending geopolitical headlines to drive downloads. Once a victim installs the fake VPN, instead of adding privacy protection it does the opposite: it delivers malware payloads such as info-stealers, remote access trojans (RATs), and banking trojans. These payloads exfiltrate sensitive data including browsing history, private messages, financial credentials, and cryptocurrency wallet information, and can give attackers remote access to the device.
redFlags: A 'VPN' app or extension promising complete anonymity or unusually broad privacy claims
Free VPN apps that request excessive permissions, such as access to contacts, messages, or storage
Apps found outside official stores, or promoted via aggressive/suggestive ads or sensational geopolitical headlines
Slight misspellings or subtle URL/branding differences from the real VPN provider's official app or website
Unverified developer names or a fraudulent 'security firm' publishing multiple similar VPN apps
realExamples: Google's November 2025 frauds and scams advisory identified threat actors distributing malicious applications disguised as legitimate VPN services across multiple platforms, impersonating trusted enterprise and consumer VPN brands.
Reported cases included a fraudulent security firm publishing malicious VPN apps on official app stores to spread malware and scams, affecting Android users globally.
Security researchers noted malicious VPN apps used sexually suggestive ads, geopolitical headlines, and fake privacy claims to lure victims into quick downloads.
reports.source: Google Safety & Security Blog, "Google's November 2025 frauds and scams advisory," https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/fraud-and-scams-advisory-november-2025/; Forbes, https://www.forbes.com/sites/daveywinder/2025/11/11/google-issues-critical-vpn-threat-warning-for-billions-of-users/

reports.title: SpyLoan Predatory Loan App Scam
reports.summary: Malicious "instant loan" apps on Google Play and the Apple App Store lure people with promises of quick cash, then harvest contacts, photos, and messages from their phones to blackmail and harass them into paying inflated fees.
safetyTips: Only download lending or finance apps from well-established, verified financial institutions and check developer legitimacy before installing
Review and deny any permission requests (contacts, photos, SMS, camera) that are not essential to a loan app's function
Verify any lender's registration with your country's financial regulator before submitting personal or banking information
Uninstall suspicious loan apps immediately, revoke their permissions, and change any passwords or PINs shared with the app
Report predatory or extortionate loan apps to the app store and to consumer protection agencies like the FTC or BBB
reports.howItWorks: Scammers publish seemingly legitimate personal-loan or finance apps on official app stores or push them through social media ads and SMS links. During setup, the app demands excessive permissions unrelated to lending, such as access to contacts, SMS history, photos, camera, and call logs. Once a "loan" is issued (often smaller than promised and with hidden fees or predatory interest), the operators use the stolen personal data to harass, publicly shame, or threaten the victim and people in their contact list in order to pressure repayment at inflated rates, turning a loan request into extortion and financial exploitation.
redFlags: App requests permissions with no clear connection to lending, such as contacts, photos, SMS, or camera access
Loan is advertised as instant, no-credit-check, with minimal documentation required
App was discovered via a social media ad or unsolicited text link rather than a trusted financial institution
Fees, interest rates, or repayment terms change after the loan is disbursed
Threats to contact or expose the borrower's friends/family if payment is late
realExamples: McAfee's mobile research team identified a global surge of 'SpyLoan' apps on Android in late 2024, flagging 15 apps that had amassed over 8 million cumulative downloads and used social engineering to extract sensitive data for extortion and harassment.

Check Point researchers reported in September 2025 that a malicious loan app called 'RapiPlata,' which had been downloaded an estimated 150,000 times from both the Google Play Store and Apple App Store before removal, exploited extensive device permissions to target users, notably in Colombia.

Google's November 2025 and June 2026 Frauds and Scams Advisories both flagged continued growth in mobile extortion via malicious banking and finance apps that request excessive permissions and use stolen data to extort and publicly shame victims.
reports.source: Check Point Research Blog, "Malicious Loan App Removed from iOS and Google Play App Store Posed Severe Risks to Users," Sept. 9, 2025, https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/malicious-loan-app-removed-from-ios-and-google-play-app-store-posed-severe-risks-to-users/; corroborated by McAfee Labs Blog (Nov. 25, 2024) and Google's November 2025 Frauds and Scams Advisory (blog.google)

reports.title: Fake Loan Approval/Follow-Up Text Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send unsolicited texts claiming to "follow up" on a large loan application (often $10,000) that the recipient never submitted, pressuring them to click a link or reply to "cancel" it and steal personal data instead.
safetyTips: Don't reply to or click links in unsolicited loan texts \u2014 delete them
Never give a Social Security number or bank account number in response to an unexpected text
Forward suspicious texts to 7726 (SPAM) and report them at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Verify any loan offer independently by contacting a lender through its official, verified website or phone number, not the one in the text
Talk to a trusted friend or family member before responding if you're unsure
If you already shared personal information, visit IdentityTheft.gov for recovery steps
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive an out-of-the-blue text saying they've been preapproved for a loan or that representatives are following up on a loan application, even though they never applied. The message creates false urgency with phrases like "this is the last step" or asks the recipient to reply YES to confirm or NO to cancel, which merely confirms the number is active. If the person calls the listed number or clicks the link, the "lender" asks for a Social Security number or bank account number to "finish" the application. In reality there is no loan and no lender; the goal is to harvest personal information for identity theft or to extract fees, and the operation frequently rotates through invented company names to dodge spam filters and negative reviews.
redFlags: An unsolicited text about a loan you never applied for
Promises of guaranteed pre-approval for a large, specific dollar amount
Requests for a Social Security number or bank account number to "complete" an application
Urgency language like "this is the last step" or instructions to reply YES/NO
A callback number embedded in the text rather than a verifiable company website
Company name that has no findable, verifiable lending license or history
realExamples: FTC Consumer Alert (Jan. 20, 2026) describing a text \"supposedly following up on a $10,000 loan application\" from someone who never applied
New Hampshire Banking Department reissued the FTC's fake loan text alert to warn state residents in January 2026

Reports describe a persistent operation using the name \"CNFI USA\" and an \"Alexis\" persona sending nearly identical pre-approval texts, with complaints filed with BBB and ScamPulse between 2025 and early 2026
Military Consumer (a federal consumer-protection site) republished the FTC guidance on spotting fake loan texts in January 2026
reports.source: Federal Trade Commission, Consumer Alert "Can you spot a fake loan text scam?" (Jan. 20, 2026), consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/01/can-you-spot-fake-loan-text-scam

reports.title: Fake Toll Road Text Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send text messages impersonating toll agencies like E-ZPass, SunPass, FasTrak, and TxTag, claiming the recipient owes money for an unpaid toll and must pay immediately via a malicious link.
safetyTips: Don't click links in unsolicited toll-payment texts; go directly to the toll agency's official website or app by typing the address yourself
Check your actual toll account balance by logging in independently or calling the agency's verified customer service number
Delete or report suspicious toll texts (forward to 7726/SPAM) and report them to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Never enter your Social Security number, full credit card number, or account login through a link sent via text
Monitor your bank and credit card statements for unauthorized charges if you've already clicked a suspicious toll link, and consider freezing your credit
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive an unsolicited SMS or iMessage claiming they have an outstanding toll balance or violation on a real regional toll system, often threatening late fees, suspended registration, or legal action if they don't pay right away. The message includes a link to a spoofed website that closely mimics the real toll agency's site, where victims are prompted to "log in" or enter payment details, Social Security numbers, or other personal data to resolve the supposed debt. Instead of paying a toll, victims hand their credit card numbers and personal information directly to criminals, who can then make fraudulent charges or commit identity theft. The scam has become the leading driver of a broader surge in government-impersonation fraud reported to the FTC.
redFlags: Unexpected text about an unpaid toll, especially if you don't use that toll road or an EZ-Pass/SunPass/FasTrak/TxTag account
Urgent, high-pressure language like 'final notice' or threats of late fees, fines, or legal action for not paying immediately
A link in the text rather than being told to log into the toll agency's official app or website directly
Generic greetings like 'Dear Customer' instead of your name or actual account/license plate details
Requests for payment via gift cards, cryptocurrency, or other non-standard payment methods
Misspellings, odd phrasing, or a sender number/domain that doesn't match the toll agency's official contact information
realExamples: The FTC reported that in 2025 it received more than 1 million imposter scam reports with losses up nearly 20% to $3.5 billion, and that government imposter scam reports rose 40%, driven in part by bogus overdue-toll texts spoofing programs like E-ZPass, SunPass, FasTrak, and TxTag.

Trend Micro documented scam text campaigns impersonating Florida's SunPass and Massachusetts' EZDriveMA toll systems that direct recipients to fake websites designed to harvest credit card numbers and Social Security numbers.

Consumer Reports and state toll authorities (including Georgia's Peach Pass, Illinois's I-Pass, and Indiana's E-ZPass) have publicly confirmed they never request personal or account information via text or email, after being impersonated in mass phishing campaigns.
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "New trends in reports of imposter scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/05/new-trends-reports-imposter-scams

reports.title: Fake Heavy Equipment & Vehicle Dealer Website Scam
reports.summary: Scammers clone or impersonate real heavy equipment, farm machinery, and vehicle dealerships with convincing fake websites and Marketplace ads, luring buyers with below-market prices and then vanishing after victims wire large payments.
safetyTips: Research the business at BBB.org or call your local BBB before sending any money
Contact the real dealership directly using a phone number or website you find independently, not one provided in the ad
Never wire money or use ACH transfer to purchase equipment or vehicles from a seller you haven't verified in person
Insist on an in-person inspection or a live video walkthrough of the actual item before paying anything
Check how recently the seller's website domain was registered using a WHOIS lookup
Verify serial numbers or VINs directly with the manufacturer or DMV rather than trusting documents the seller provides
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters build a professional-looking website (or Facebook Marketplace ad) that copies the name, logo, photos, and even fabricated regulatory license numbers of a real, often long-established or now-closed, equipment or vehicle dealership. They list tractors, excavators, skid steers, trucks, or cars at prices noticeably below market value to create urgency. When a buyer inquires, the "seller" provides wiring or ACH instructions, sometimes sending a fake shipping confirmation, invoice, or even a real-looking VIN, and pressures the buyer to pay quickly, often before ever seeing the equipment in person. Once payment clears, the scammers cut off phone and email contact, the equipment never arrives, and the buyer discovers the impersonated business had no knowledge of the sale. In some cases scammers use compromised servers to run dozens of similar fake dealer sites simultaneously, each claiming to be based in a different U.S. region, and some have even tried filing false business update requests with the BBB to shift blame onto uninvolved local companies.
redFlags: Price is well below market value for the make, model, or equipment type
Seller insists on wire transfer or ACH payment and refuses other secure payment methods
Seller avoids phone calls or video verification and won't allow an in-person inspection before payment
Website or ad was created very recently, or contact information doesn't match the real dealership's official listing
Seller becomes unreachable (disconnected phone, bounced email) immediately after payment is sent
Listing photos and descriptions appear identical across multiple unrelated 'dealer' websites
realExamples: BBB warned that a fake online retailer impersonating Missouri's Cook Equipment & Trucking cost consumers nationwide more than $223,000, including a $45,000 loss on a skid steer loader in Oak Hills, California
BBB investigation found the fraudulent website 'Rock Line Equipment' had hijacked the identities of two legitimate Kansas businesses and was linked to at least $51,000 in reported losses
An Arizona woman wired $76,015 to 'Nations Remarketing Group,' a car auction site using a stolen Kansas business identity, after scammers sent a fake shipping confirmation before going silent

A nationwide BBB study found over 200 Scam Tracker reports since 2022 plus 140 additional complaints involving fake vehicle and heavy equipment dealer websites, including one Lithuania-based server hosting nearly 30 fraudulent sites impersonating businesses across multiple states
reports.source: Better Business Bureau, "BBB Study: Impostor scammers target consumers, businesses and BBB," https://www.bbb.org/article/news-releases/31436-bbb-study-watch-out-for-vehicle-and-equipment-impostor-scams; and "BBB Scam Alert: BBB warns of online equipment scam, impersonating Missouri dealer," https://www.bbb.org/article/scams/32122-bbb-warns-of-online-equipment-scam-impersonating-missouri-dealer

reports.title: SEO Poisoning Bank Account Takeover Scam
reports.summary: Criminals buy fake search-engine ads or build lookalike phishing sites that outrank real bank, payroll, and health savings account login pages, then trick victims into handing over passwords and one-time codes to drain their accounts.
relatedScams: Financial Institution Support Impersonation Account Takeover Scam
safetyTips: Never provide login credentials, passwords, or one-time passcodes to anyone who contacts you, even if they claim to be from your bank
Navigate directly to your financial institution's website by typing the known URL yourself rather than clicking search ads or links
If a caller claims to be from your bank, hang up and call back using the number on the back of your card or official statement
Enable strong, unique passwords and multi-factor authentication, and avoid posting personal details online that could help attackers guess security answers
Report suspected account takeover attempts to your financial institution immediately and file a complaint with IC3.gov using the keywords 'account takeover' or 'SEO poisoning'
reports.howItWorks: Scammers use a technique called "SEO poisoning," purchasing search ads or optimizing fraudulent pages so they appear above or alongside a real financial institution's website when someone searches for their bank's login or customer support number. Victims click the fake ad or link, land on a convincing clone of the real site or speak to a fake "support" agent, and are manipulated through social engineering (calls, texts, emails, or fraudulent websites) into revealing login credentials, multi-factor authentication codes, or one-time passcodes. Once criminals gain account access, they quickly wire funds to other criminal-controlled accounts, many linked to cryptocurrency wallets, making the money extremely difficult to recover. The scheme targets not just personal bank accounts but also business accounts, payroll systems, and health savings accounts.
redFlags: An unsolicited call, text, or email from someone claiming to be your bank's support staff asking you to verify login credentials, MFA codes, or OTPs
Search results or ads for your bank's 'customer service number' or login page that look slightly different from the official URL
Being asked to read back a one-time passcode or multi-factor authentication code to 'verify your identity'
Urgent pressure to act immediately on a supposed account problem, fraud alert, or login issue
A support number found via a search engine ad rather than the number printed on your card or official bank statement
realExamples: FBI IC3 issued PSA I-112525-PSA on November 25, 2025 warning that since January 2025 it received more than 5,100 complaints of account takeover fraud via financial institution impersonation, with losses exceeding $262 million

Cybercriminals purchased search ads mimicking legitimate bank ads so fraudulent phishing sites ranked prominently in search results, tricking users searching for their bank's website into entering login information

Reports describe attackers impersonating financial institution, payroll provider, and health savings account support staff via calls, texts, emails, and social media/forums to obtain credentials and MFA/OTP codes before wiring stolen funds to crypto wallets
reports.source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), Public Service Announcement I-112525-PSA, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251125

reports.title: FTC Impersonator Fake Employee ID Refund Recovery Scam
reports.summary: Scammers text or WhatsApp victims claiming to be FTC "agents" who can help recover money lost in a previous scam, sending a photo of a fake employee badge/ID to seem legitimate before stealing money or financial data.
relatedScams: FTC Official Impersonation Bitcoin ATM Scam
safetyTips: Remember a real FTC employee will never contact you by text or messaging app to discuss a case or refund
Know that the FTC never texts photos of employee IDs or badges to 'verify' identity
Never pay a fee, wire money, or send crypto/gift cards to anyone claiming they can recover scam losses
Do not share bank account numbers or Social Security numbers with unsolicited contacts claiming to be government officials
Verify by going directly to official FTC.gov contact channels rather than replying to the text or calling numbers it provides
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters contact people—often those who already lost money to an earlier scam or filed a fraud report—via text message or a messaging app like WhatsApp, claiming to be an FTC employee or "agent" who can help recover their prior losses. To build trust, the scammer sends a photo of what looks like an official government employee ID card and badge, all of which are fabricated. Once the victim is convinced, the scammer asks them to pay a fee, move money into an account the scammer controls, or hand over bank account or Social Security information supposedly needed to process the "refund." In reality the FTC has no such recovery agents, never initiates contact this way, and the victim's money or data is simply stolen.
redFlags: Contact by text message or WhatsApp from someone claiming to be an FTC employee or 'agent'
Being sent a photo of an employee ID or badge as 'proof' of identity
Any claim that a government employee can personally help recover money lost in a past scam
Requests to pay a fee, move money to a specified account, or share bank/Social Security details to receive a refund
Urgency or pressure to act quickly to 'secure' recovered funds
realExamples: FTC consumer alert describing victims receiving texts from people claiming to be FTC employees who send fake photo IDs and badges before requesting money or financial information for a bogus refund/recovery service
Consumer coverage describing the scam specifically targeting people who had already reported being defrauded, exploiting their hope of recovering losses
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "A real FTC employee won't text you their photo ID to 'verify' their identity," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/06/real-ftc-employee-wont-text-you-their-photo-id-verify-their-identity

reports.title: Refund and Recovery "Sucker List" Scam
reports.summary: Scammers buy and sell lists of people who were previously defrauded, then pose as government agencies, law firms, or consumer groups offering to recover the victim's lost money for an upfront fee — draining them a second time.
relatedScams: FTC Impersonator Fake Employee ID Refund Recovery Scam
safetyTips: Never pay an upfront fee or give financial/personal information to get a refund "no legitimate government agency or company requires this
If someone contacts you claiming to be from a government agency or law firm about a past scam, independently look up and call that organization directly rather than using contact info they provide
Search the organization's name online along with words like 'complaint,' 'scam,' or 'review' before engaging further
Be skeptical of any unsolicited call, text, email, or social media message referencing a scam you previously fell for
Avoid searching online for 'scam recovery' or similar help services, as this can lead directly to more recovery scammers
Report suspected refund/recovery scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: After someone falls for an initial scam, their contact details and information about how they were scammed often end up on a "sucker list" that fraud rings buy and sell. A new scammer then calls, emails, texts, messages on social media, or mails a letter claiming they can help recover the money, prize, or merchandise the person lost. They may claim to be from a federal agency like the FTC, a consumer advocacy group, a law firm, or even the original scammy company offering refunds to "dissatisfied customers." Because they already know details of the original fraud, their pitch sounds credible. Before "releasing" the recovered funds, they ask the victim to pay an upfront "retainer fee," "processing fee," "administrative charge," "tax," or "shipping and handling charge," or to hand over a Social Security number or bank/debit account information — which the scammer then uses to steal money or commit identity theft. The FTC also warns scammers are now using AI to make these pitches look and sound more legitimate.
redFlags: Someone contacts you out of the blue claiming they can recover money you lost to a past scam
You're asked to pay any kind of upfront fee, 'tax,' or 'processing charge' before receiving a promised refund
The caller already knows details about a prior scam you experienced and uses that to build trust
They ask for your Social Security number, bank account, or other financial/personal information to 'process' the refund
They pressure you to pay via cash, gift cards, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer
They claim to guarantee they can get your name 'to the top of a list' for reimbursement
realExamples: FTC consumer alert describes scammers buying lists of previously defrauded people that include names, addresses, phone numbers, the type of scam used, and how much the victim paid.
News outlets reported scammers posing as federal agencies, consumer advocacy groups, or law firms and asking for upfront fees or financial information to 'recover' lost funds.
A regional TV consumer report quoted an FTC official warning that scammers are increasingly using AI to look and sound more legitimate when running these refund/recovery pitches.
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Refund and Recovery Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/refund-and-recovery-scams

reports.title: Financial Institution Support Impersonation Account Takeover Scam
reports.summary: The FBI warns that criminals are impersonating banks, payroll providers, and health savings account (HSA) administrators to trick people into handing over login credentials and one-time passcodes, then draining or hijacking the accounts.
relatedScams: SEO Poisoning Bank Account Takeover Scam
safetyTips: Never share your login credentials, MFA codes, or one-time passcodes with anyone who contacts you, even if they claim to be from your bank or employer
Contact your financial institution, payroll provider, or HSA administrator directly using a phone number or website you look up yourself, not one provided in the suspicious message

If you suspect your account was accessed, contact your financial institution immediately to request a recall or reversal and a Hold Harmless Letter, and reset all potentially exposed credentials and passwords, including on other sites where you reused them

Report suspected account takeover fraud to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov, including the words 'Account Takeover' or 'SEO poisoning' in the description, and notify the impersonated company so it can warn others
reports.howItWorks: Criminals pose as a financial institution's support staff or replicate its website, then use texts, phone calls, emails, or fraudulent lookalike websites to manipulate the account holder into giving up login credentials, multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes, or one-time passcodes (OTPs). Once the criminal has this information, they log into the victim's actual online banking, payroll, or health savings account and use the access to steal funds, redirect paychecks, or otherwise move money out of the victim's control. The scheme targets individuals as well as businesses and organizations of all sizes across sectors, not just personal bank customers.
redFlags: Unsolicited text, call, or email claiming to be from your bank, payroll provider, or HSA administrator asking you to verify your login or share a code
A request for your multi-factor authentication code or one-time passcode over the phone or via text/email
Being directed to click a link or download software to 'resolve' an account issue rather than logging in directly through the official app or website
A sense of urgency pushing you to act immediately to 'secure' or 'verify' your account
Slight misspellings or odd URLs in a bank/payroll website link sent to you
realExamples: FBI IC3 reports that since January 2025 it received more than 5,100 complaints of account takeover (ATO) fraud via impersonation of financial institution support, with losses exceeding $262 million
Cyber criminals impersonate a financial institution's staff or website to gain access, often reaching victims through social engineering via texts, calls, and emails or through fraudulent websites
The scheme has been used to gain unauthorized access not just to bank accounts but also to targeted payroll and health savings accounts
reports.source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), PSA I-112525-PSA, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251125

reports.title: Health Insurer + Chinese Law Enforcement Impersonation Extortion Scam
reports.summary: The FBI warns that criminals are targeting Chinese-speaking residents of the U.S. by impersonating health insurance claims departments and then handing the call off to fake Chinese police who threaten extradition unless the victim pays "bail."
relatedScams: Gold Bar & Bulk Cash Courier Scam
safetyTips: Independently verify any health insurance claim by using the phone number or website printed on your insurance card, not one given by the caller
Do not share personal information, including health insurance account logins, with an unsolicited caller
Never wire money or pay 'bail' to anyone who calls you, especially foreign law enforcement claiming jurisdiction over a US resident
Do not install video communication software or allow anyone to maintain live video access to your device
Hang up and report the call to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) with any phone numbers, names, or transaction details
reports.howItWorks: According to an FBI/IC3 public service announcement, targeted individuals receive a call from a spoofed telephone number belonging to a legitimate U.S. health insurance provider's claims department, conducted in Chinese, asking about recent insurance claims for alleged surgical procedures; the criminal then shows the recipient fraudulent invoices on screen via video communication software and demands payment. If the recipient denies filing the claim, the criminal transfers them to someone posing as Chinese law enforcement, who asks for personal identifying information, threatens extradition or foreign prosecution, and demands a large payment for bail, and may instruct the victim to download video communication software and stay connected for 24-hour "surveillance."
redFlags: An unsolicited call in Chinese claiming to be from a health insurer's claims department about a surgery you never had
Being shown invoices over video call and pressured to pay immediately
A second caller claiming to be Chinese police who demands personal ID information and a 'bail' payment
Instructions to download video software and stay connected around the clock for 'surveillance'
Threats of extradition or foreign prosecution over an insurance dispute
realExamples: FBI/IC3 PSA describing victims receiving spoofed calls from a health insurer's claims department in Chinese, being shown fraudulent invoices via video software, then transferred to a fake Chinese law enforcement officer demanding bail payment and personal ID information
Reports describe scammers instructing victims to maintain 24-hour video connectivity for 'surveillance' after the extortion call
reports.source: FBI/IC3, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251113

reports.title: Virtual Casting Call Text Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send unsolicited texts posing as talent scouts offering movie or TV auditions, then pressure victims into paying for fake photo shoots or acting classes.
safetyTips: Never respond to unexpected texts about acting jobs or casting calls
Remember that legitimate talent agencies find jobs for you and pay you after the client pays them, rather than charging you upfront
Report unwanted texts to 7726 (SPAM) or use your phone's 'report junk' feature, then delete the message
Report the scam to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Independently verify any casting opportunity by contacting the studio or a known talent agency directly rather than using contact info from the text
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive an unexpected text message from a supposed "talent scout" claiming they've been selected for a virtual audition tied to a well-known movie or television show. The message asks if the recipient is available for a casting call they never actually signed up for. Anyone who responds may be routed into a "virtual audition" that turns out to be a high-pressure sales pitch to enroll in bogus paid photo shoots or fake acting classes, with the scammer eventually asking for payment or bank information as a supposed condition of participating in the casting.
redFlags: An unexpected text about an audition or casting call you never applied for
Being asked to pay for test shoots, headshots, or to 'secure your spot' before any job is confirmed
High-pressure sales pitch during a so-called virtual audition
Requests for bank information tied to participating in a casting call
Name-dropping specific popular movies or shows to seem credible
realExamples: FTC's Military Consumer program described texts from a fake 'talent scout' offering auditions for a well-known movie like 'The Devil Wears Prada 2' or a show like 'Ted Lasso,' asking recipients if they were still available for a virtual open call they never signed up for.
reports.source: Military Consumer (FTC-affiliated), https://www.militaryconsumer.gov/blog/lights-camera-scam-spot-virtual-casting-call-scams

reports.title: Brushing Scam with QR Code Twist
reports.summary: Scammers ship you a cheap, unordered item using your real name and address so they can post a fake "verified buyer" review under your identity, and increasingly tuck in a QR code that claims to help you identify the sender or process a return but actually leads to a phishing site.
safetyTips: Do not scan any QR code included inside an unexpected package — a legitimate retailer or delivery service never needs this to identify a sender or process a return
You are not legally obligated to pay for or return items you never ordered — you can keep them
If the package appears to be from Amazon or another online marketplace, report it to that platform so they can investigate the seller
Check your accounts on online marketplaces for reviews posted under your name that you didn't write
Report a brushing scam to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: An unexpected package shows up at your door that you never ordered, often containing something cheap and random like baby wipes, toothpaste, or seeds. It may look like it's from a known company like Amazon, or from a person or business you've never heard of. A third-party seller has obtained your name and address without your consent and shipped you the item so the delivery gives them a real tracking number and "proof" of a completed sale, which they use to post a fake five-star review under your name to "brush up" their own ratings. In a newer twist, the package includes a note with a QR code telling you to scan it to find out who sent the package or to process a return — scanning it instead leads to a phishing site designed to steal credit card numbers, usernames, and passwords.
redFlags: An unexpected, unordered package arrives addressed to you containing a cheap, random item
The sender is a business or person you don't recognize, or the package claims to be from a company like Amazon with no order history to match
A note inside asks you to scan a QR code to find out who sent it or to process a return
You later find a five-star review posted under your name for a product you never bought
realExamples: The FTC's own August 2026 consumer alert describes recent reports of packages containing cheap, random items like baby wipes, toothpaste, or seeds, used to generate delivery confirmations for fake reviews

That same FTC alert warns that some of these packages include a note with a QR code claiming to help identify the sender or process a return, which instead leads to a phishing site built to steal credit card numbers, usernames, and passwords
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Did you get a package you didn't order? It could be a brushing scam," August 2026, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/08/unexpected-package-you-got-could-be-brushing-scam

reports.title: "Veterans Savings Program" Postcard Scam
reports.summary: Scammers mail veterans official-looking postcards claiming they qualify for extra money through a fake "Veterans Savings Program," name-dropping real VA benefits like CHAMPVA or TRICARE For Life to seem legitimate, and pressuring them to call a number and hand over Social Security and bank details.
safetyTips: Do not call the number printed on the postcard — contact the VA Benefits Hotline directly at 1-800-827-1000 instead
Never give your Social Security number or bank details to someone who contacted you first
Remember that legitimate VA communications will not pressure you to respond immediately or share sensitive information over the phone
Verify any benefit offer by going directly to VA.gov or calling a number you already know is real
Report suspicious postcards to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to the VA at VSAFE.gov or 1-833-38V-SAFE
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters send physical postcards to veterans that mimic official VA mail, referencing real benefit programs like CHAMPVA or TRICARE For Life and listing the veteran's home state to appear legitimate. The postcard promises "extra money" through a so-called Veterans Savings Program, which does not actually exist, and urges the recipient to call a phone number right away or risk losing out. Once a veteran calls, the scammer on the line pressures them to provide sensitive information such as their Social Security number or bank account details under the guise of processing the "benefit."
redFlags: Postcard advertises a "Veterans Savings Program" — a program that does not actually exist
Message creates urgency, insisting you call right away or lose out on funds
Request to call an unfamiliar phone number rather than contacting the VA directly
Caller asks for a Social Security number or bank account information over the phone
Mail mimics real VA benefit names, like CHAMPVA or TRICARE For Life, to appear more legitimate
realExamples: The FTC's own August 2026 consumer alert describes veterans across the country reporting these postcards, confirming the "Veterans Savings Program" named on them does not exist and is being used purely to phish for personal and financial information

The same FTC alert notes scammers are increasingly pretending to be affiliated with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and directs anyone who receives one of these postcards to verify benefits only through a number they already know is real, such as the VA benefits hotline
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "How to spot a postcard scam targeting veterans," August 2026, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/08/how-spot-postcard-scam-targeting-veterans

reports.title: Car Wrap Advertising Scam
reports.summary: Scammers offer people hundreds of dollars a week to drive around with their car wrapped in a major brand's advertising, then send a fake cashier's check that leaves victims owing the bank money after they wire funds to a "vendor."
relatedScams: Fake Check Scam Targeting Childcare Providers
safetyTips: Never spend money from a deposited check or send any of it elsewhere before the check has fully cleared, which can take weeks even if the funds appear available sooner

Know that banks are allowed to make a check's funds available before the transfer is actually verified — a check can look "cleared" and spendable for days before the bank discovers it's fake and reverses it
Contact the brand named in the ad directly through its official website to verify whether it actually runs a car wrap advertising program
Only use payment apps like Venmo or Cash App to send money to people you personally know, never a "vendor" a stranger tells you to pay
Report suspected car wrap scams to BBB Scam Tracker and the FTC
reports.howItWorks: A victim sees an ad or gets a text claiming a major brand will pay them hundreds of dollars a week to wrap their car in company advertising. After filling out an application, a "boss" contacts them by text with instructions and mails a cashier's check meant to cover the cost of installing the wrap. The victim is told to deposit the check and use part of it to pay a specific "local vendor" via Venmo or Cash App who will supposedly install the wrap. Because the check initially appears to clear, the victim sends real money to the scammer-controlled vendor before the bank discovers the check is counterfeit, leaving the victim responsible for repaying the full fake amount.
redFlags: Unsolicited offer to pay hundreds of dollars a week just for driving with an ad wrap on your car
You're sent a check and told to deposit it, then immediately send part of the money elsewhere via Venmo or Cash App
The employer contacts you only through text message and never in person or via a verifiable company channel
You never met the "vendor" and were told exactly which one to pay
The job requires no interview and pays out before any actual work (driving/advertising) has occurred
realExamples: In BBB's own reporting, one victim described the scam directly: told to deposit the check and pay a vendor through Venmo once it cleared, they sent $3,500 — then waited two days for someone to come wrap their car. No one ever came, and the vendor kept making excuses when contacted.
reports.source: Better Business Bureau, "BBB Scam Alert: Car wrap scams hook job seekers with promise of easy money," February 19, 2021, https://www.bbb.org/article/news-releases/17538-bbb-urges-people-to-be-wary-of-promises-of-easy-money-in-vehicle-wrap-schemes

reports.title: Fake Online Pet Sale Scam
reports.summary: Scammers post fake ads for puppies and other pets, often priced far below what the breed normally costs, then demand upfront payment through untraceable methods before disappearing without ever delivering an animal.
safetyTips: Research the seller by searching their name or business online along with words like "review," "scam," or "complaint"
Watch how you're asked to pay — only scammers insist on gift cards, a payment app, cryptocurrency, or a wire transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram, since that money is hard to get back
Consider adopting from a local rescue or animal shelter instead, where you can often adopt for a small fee
If you already sent money to a scammer, look up what steps you can still take to try to recover it
Report suspected pet scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: Scammers post ads, particularly for puppies, on social media, online marketplaces, or streetcorner flyers, using an appealing photo to draw buyers in. The animals are often priced at a few hundred dollars when that breed would normally cost thousands, and the listing pressures buyers to act fast before the pet is gone. The scammer insists on payment up front, before any in-person meeting or video call with the animal. Once payment is sent, the buyer never receives the pet, who may not even exist, and the money is gone for good.
redFlags: Seller insists on payment before you can see or meet the pet in person or by video
Price seems far below what that breed normally costs, and the seller pushes you to act fast before it's gone
Payment is only accepted via gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or a wire transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram
Little or no information available when you search the seller's name or business online
realExamples: The FTC's own December 2024 consumer alert describes exactly this pattern: purebred puppies advertised for a few hundred dollars when they typically cost thousands, with sellers pushing buyers to act fast before the animal goes to someone else

The same FTC alert warns that paying with a gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer service is the clearest sign of a scam, since those payment methods are specifically what make it so hard to ever get the money back
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Getting a pet? Avoid scams," December 2024, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/12/getting-pet-avoid-scams

reports.title: Disaster Recovery Contractor Scam
reports.summary: After a hurricane, wildfire, tornado, or other disaster, unlicensed contractors show up in the recovery zone promising fast repairs, demand full payment up front through hard-to-trace methods, and either vanish or leave the work unfinished.
safetyTips: Check out a contractor's reputation on trusted review sites and by searching their name online with words like "scam," "review," or "complaint" before you commit
Confirm the contractor's license and insurance with your state or county government, and ask for proof of insurance directly
Get written estimates from more than one contractor, each listing the work, materials, completion date, price, and the contractor's contact information
Get everything in a written contract, and never sign a blank one
Pay by credit card or check only — never by wire transfer, gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or cash
Never sign your insurance check over to a contractor; arrange with your bank or credit union for a certificate of completion so the contractor is paid in stages as you approve the work
Remember FEMA never charges an application fee — anyone who wants money to help you qualify for FEMA relief is running a scam
reports.howItWorks: In the days after a hurricane, wildfire, tornado, or other disaster, unlicensed contractors and scammers appear in the recovery zone offering immediate clean-up or repairs. They tell homeowners they don't need to be licensed to do the work, offer a discount if the homeowner signs a contract right away, and sometimes ask the homeowner to sign over their insurance check directly to them. They ask for full payment up front, insisting on wire transfer, gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or cash rather than a credit card or check, and may ask the homeowner to sign a "blank contract" or suggest borrowing from a lender the contractor knows. A related version of the scam involves someone offering to help a disaster victim qualify for FEMA relief funds for a fee — FEMA does not charge application fees, so any such offer is a scam. After collecting payment, the scammer may do substandard work, disappear before finishing, or never start at all.
redFlags: The contractor claims they don't need to be licensed to do the work
You're offered a discount only if you sign a contract immediately
You're asked to sign your insurance check over to the contractor
Full payment is demanded up front, before any work begins
The contractor insists on wire transfer, gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or cash instead of a credit card or check
You're asked to sign a blank contract
Someone offers to help you qualify for FEMA relief funds for a fee
realExamples: The FTC's own consumer guidance on disaster recovery scams lists signing over an insurance check and signing a "blank contract" as specific tactics scammers use on homeowners rebuilding after a storm
The same FTC guidance states directly that FEMA doesn't charge application fees, and that anyone asking for money to help a disaster victim qualify for FEMA funds is running a scam
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "How To Avoid Scams After Weather Emergencies and Natural Disasters," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-avoid-scams-after-weather-emergencies-and-natural-disasters

reports.title: Tariff Rebate / "Tariff Dividend" Check Scam
reports.summary: Scammers are exploiting news coverage of proposed $2,000 "tariff dividend" or rebate checks by sending fake texts, emails, and even fraudulent paper checks claiming recipients must act immediately to claim tariff-related refund money.
safetyTips: Remember that government agencies do not send texts offering money or demanding a response to qualify for a payment
Know that no tariff rebate/dividend program has actually been approved by Congress, so any message claiming to pay one out is fraudulent
Never click links in unsolicited refund texts or emails; go directly to official government websites instead
If you receive a surprise check, don't deposit it or send money back before verifying its legitimacy with your bank and the relevant agency
Report suspicious tariff refund messages to your state attorney general's consumer protection division
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters send unsolicited texts, emails, or social media messages claiming the recipient is owed a "tariff refund" or "tariff dividend," a hook made believable by real news coverage of a proposed $2,000 rebate tied to tariff income. The messages use bold, capitalized language and false deadlines to pressure victims into clicking a link and entering personal or banking information, or in some variants, victims receive an actual paper check in the mail and are told to deposit it and wire back a portion for "fees" or "processing" before the check later bounces. Scammers count on the fact that most people don't understand how legitimate customs or tariff refunds actually work, since real refunds require formal filings and documentation and are never issued spontaneously via unsolicited text.
redFlags: An unexpected message about a tariff refund or rebate arriving by text, email, or social media rather than official government mail
Bold, capitalized wording and an urgent deadline claiming the check will be withheld or expire if you don't act immediately
A request to click a link and provide personal information or bank details to "claim" the money
A surprise paper check arriving despite never filing any claim or paperwork
Instructions to deposit a check and send back part of the funds for fees or processing
realExamples: Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador's office warned residents in late 2025/early 2026 about text messages telling recipients they must click a link and provide personal information to collect a $2,000 tariff rebate check, even though no such policy has been approved by Congress
The Idaho Attorney General's office described the scam texts as featuring bold, capitalized words claiming the recipient's check would be withheld unless they clicked a link and responded immediately
Consumer-facing reporting identified fake tariff refund/rebate checks as a distinct scam type where victims are told to deposit a check and send back part of the funds for "fees" or "processing"
reports.source: Idaho Office of the Attorney General, https://www.ag.idaho.gov/newsroom/attorney-general-labrador-warns-idahoans-about-tariff-rebate-text-scam/ ; Kitsap Credit Union, https://kitsapcu.org/blog/tariff-refund-scams-what-you-need-to-know/

reports.title: Utility Company Shutoff Scam
reports.summary: Scammers pose as your gas, electric, or water company and threaten to shut off your service unless you pay immediately, usually by wire transfer, gift card, payment app, or cryptocurrency.
safetyTips: Know that real utility companies will not demand immediate payment to avoid same-day disconnection
Hang up, and contact your utility yourself using the number on your bill or the company website, never a number the caller gave you
Never pay anyone who demands payment by wire transfer, gift card, cryptocurrency, or payment app
When searching online for your utility, scroll past the paid ads at the top, since some impersonate real utility companies
Report utility scams to your real utility company, to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and to your state attorney general
reports.howItWorks: Someone calls, texts, emails, or even shows up at your door claiming to be from your gas, electric, or water company. They say you have a past-due bill and that your service will be shut off unless you pay right away, sometimes the same day. The goal is to scare you into paying before you have time to check. They insist you can only pay one way, such as wiring money through Western Union or MoneyGram, buying gift cards and reading them the numbers on the back, using a payment app, or sending cryptocurrency, because that money is hard to get back. After big storms and power outages, scammers also send messages that look like they come from your utility, with links designed to steal your personal information, sometimes promising to restore your service faster if you pay.
redFlags: A threat to shut off your gas, electric, or water service unless you pay immediately
A caller who insists you have a past-due bill even though you know you already paid
Being told you can only pay by wire transfer, gift card, cash reload card, payment app, or cryptocurrency
A request for your banking information by phone or email
A message after a storm or outage offering to restore your service faster if you pay or share your information
realExamples: In September 2018 the FTC warned it had been hearing about scammers impersonating utility companies, calling to say electricity or water would be shut off unless a past-due bill was paid, with small businesses among the targets

In January 2026, after a winter storm left hundreds of thousands without power, the FTC warned of messages that looked like they came from utility companies, with links designed to steal personal information and false promises of faster service restoration for payment
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/scammers-pretend-be-your-utility-company ; FTC Consumer Alert (Jan 2026), https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/01/avoid-weather-related-utility-scams-after-recent-winter-storm ; FTC Consumer Alert (Sep 2018), https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2018/09/empower-yourself-against-utility-scams

reports.title: Fake Social Security Statement Email Scam
reports.summary: Scammers are mass-emailing fake notices claiming your Social Security statement is ready to download, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links or opening attachments. The SSA's Office of Inspector General warns this is a surge in government imposter phishing, separate from phone-based SSN "suspension" scams.
safetyTips: Do not click links or open attachments in unsolicited emails claiming to be from SSA
Go directly to ssa.gov/myaccount to access or set up your real Social Security account rather than using any link in an email
Verify that any official SSA email address ends in '.gov' before trusting it
If you clicked a link or shared information, stop all contact with the sender, contact your financial institutions, and report the incident to SSA OIG, the FBI's IC3, and the FTC
Report suspicious emails immediately to the SSA Office of Inspector General
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive an unsolicited email designed to look like an official Social Security Administration message, complete with government-style logos, colors, and formatting, claiming their Social Security statement is ready to view or download. The email contains a link or attachment labeled as the official document; clicking it can install malware on the victim's device or redirect them to a fake website designed to harvest personal and financial information, which can then be used for identity theft or financial fraud.
redFlags: Unsolicited email claiming your Social Security statement is ready to download
Embedded links or attachments labeled as official statements or documents
Sender email address does not end in '.gov'
Message creates urgency or pressure to act immediately
Requests to pay via gift cards, prepaid debit cards, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, cash, or gold bars, or threats of arrest/benefit suspension
realExamples: SSA OIG issued a February 19, 2026 nationwide scam alert describing a 'significant increase in government imposter scam emails' falsely offering access to a Social Security statement
SSA OIG noted the fake emails use official-looking logos, colors, and formatting and that links may install malware or direct victims to fake data-harvesting websites
reports.source: SSA Office of the Inspector General, https://oig.ssa.gov/scam-alerts/2026-02-20-ssa-office-of-the-inspector-general-warns-public-of-surge-in-fraudulent-social-security-statement-emails/

reports.title: Timeshare Resale Scam
reports.summary: Scammers target timeshare owners trying to sell, promising a quick sale at a big price if the owner first pays an upfront "registration" or closing fee — then the company disappears with the money.
safetyTips: Never pay any fee upfront to a timeshare reseller — it's better to do business with a reseller that takes fees only after the sale is complete
Check out the reseller with the state attorney general and local consumer protection agency where the company is located, and search their name online with words like "complaint" or "scam"
Confirm the reseller's agents are licensed to sell real estate in the state where your timeshare is located
Be skeptical of guarantees of fast sales, ready buyers, or big guaranteed returns — these are classic signs of a scam
reports.howItWorks: Timeshare owners who want to sell receive unsolicited calls or emails from people posing as resale agents who claim to have eager buyers lined up, often "big-name companies" wanting the timeshare for business travel or events, and who guarantee a fast sale at a hefty price. Before the "deal" can close, the company says the owner must pay several hundred to a couple thousand dollars via credit card for "registration," listing, advertising, or closing fees. Once the fee is paid, the promised sale never happens — the company's promises of ready buyers, fast sales, big profits and money-back guarantees turn out to be lies, and owners are left stuck with credit card debt from paying the fee.
redFlags: A caller or company claims the market for your timeshare is "hot" and they're "overwhelmed" with eager buyers
You're told they already have a buyer ready to purchase, or they promise to sell your timeshare within a specific short timeframe
You're asked to pay an upfront fee (reported as $500-$2,000) by credit card before any sale closes, sometimes labeled "registration" or closing costs
They promise a money-back guarantee if the resale doesn't go through
The company doesn't provide a contract, or provides one that doesn't accurately reflect the conversations you had
realExamples: FTC's 2014 consumer alert describes a company, Vacation Property Services, that claimed to represent big-name companies eager to buy timeshares for business travel and events and guaranteed owners hefty returns, then charged $500 to $2,000 in "registration" fees before disappearing
reports.source: FTC, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2014/05/be-lookout-timeshare-resale-phonies; FTC, https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/timeshares-vacation-clubs-and-related-scams; FBI New York, https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/newyork/news/fbi-new-york-warns-of-scams-targeting-timeshare-owners

reports.title: Home Title Lock Insurance Scam
reports.summary: Ads warn homeowners that criminals can steal their home's title and push them to buy "title lock insurance," but the FTC says this product is neither a lock nor insurance and won't actually prevent title fraud.
safetyTips: Remember title fraud is a form of identity theft, not a product real insurance covers
Check your property title for free through your state or county's land records office
Sign up for your area's free title/deed change notification program if one is available, instead of paying a monthly fee
Take a breath before reacting to scary ads "Stop. Take a breath. It's just a ploy to scare you." and research any company before paying
reports.howItWorks: Companies run scary ads claiming thieves can steal the title to your home, designed to frighten homeowners into buying "title lock insurance."
