According to the FTC, "title lock insurance" is not title insurance, which protects you against challenges to the title, like a lien you didn't know about
redFlags: Ads that claim thieves can easily steal your home's title and create panic to sell a product
A service calling itself 'insurance' or a 'lock' that doesn't actually prevent fraud or restore a stolen title
Marketing that conflates 'title lock insurance' with real title insurance
Pressure to subscribe to paid monitoring instead of being told about free alternatives
realExamples: FTC consumer alert describing ads that tell homeowners thieves can steal their home's title and then pitch 'title lock insurance' as the fix
Consumers commenting on the FTC's alert page describe seeing TV commercials that caused panic, with real estate lawyers telling them they'd never heard of an actual title-theft case
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/08/home-title-lock-insurance-not-lock-all

reports.title: Fake Vehicle History Report Scam for Car Sellers
reports.summary: Scammers posing as interested car buyers on sites like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist pressure sellers into purchasing a "vehicle history report" from an unfamiliar website, which actually steals the seller's credit card and personal information.
safetyTips: Do not click buyer-sent links; these often lead to phishing sites or hidden malware downloads

Never enter payment info on unfamiliar sites " if a buyer insists you use a website you've never heard of, stop immediately and verify the site's legitimacy before sharing any financial or personal details
Stick to established, trusted report services like Carfax, AutoCheck, or NMVTIS
Include your vehicle's VIN in your ad so genuine buyers can run their own reports without needing your involvement
Report suspicious messages directly to the platform and to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov
If you already paid on a fake site, contact your bank right away, cancel the card, and monitor your account for unauthorized charges
reports.howItWorks: A person responds to an online car listing claiming to be a serious buyer, often opening with a vague or friendly message to build rapport. Before "finalizing" the purchase, they ask the seller to first obtain a vehicle history report from a specific, unfamiliar service (such as one called "ASR" or "Auto Smart Report") rather than a trusted service like Carfax, AutoCheck, or NMVTIS. The site looks professional, promising something like a "complete vehicle history at your fingertips," but when the seller enters their personal details and credit card number to pay for the report, the information is harvested by criminals rather than used to generate a real report. The "buyer" may also raise the offer price to keep the seller engaged, but once payment is made on the fake site, the buyer disappears, having never intended to purchase the vehicle at all.
redFlags: A buyer who asks you to get a report from an unknown service like "ASR" instead of accepting a Carfax, AutoCheck, or NMVTIS report
Messages that ignore your ad details, such as short, nonsensical first contact or questions showing they haven't read the listing
Offers above your asking price
Phrases like "will you accept cash?" or "I just need to see a report first"
Generic greetings like "dear," "brother," or "friend"
realExamples: A seller named Nick K. of Washington shared his Craigslist listing and vehicle details with a buyer, who replied asking him to get an "Auto Smart Report" from a specific link, then upped his cash offer by $500 to pressure Nick into paying for the report before any sale was finalized.
reports.source: Fox News, https://www.foxnews.com/tech/craigslist-car-report-scam-targets-vehicle-sellers

reports.title: Auto Warranty Robocall Scam
reports.summary: Illegal recorded robocalls claim your car's manufacturer warranty is about to expire and pressure you to "renew" it, but the call isn't from your dealer or manufacturer and the product is an overpriced, often worthless service contract.
safetyTips: Hang up immediately and don't press any numbers, engaging can lead to more calls
Use a call-blocking app or device to filter unwanted robocalls
Report the robocall at DoNotCall.gov
reports.howItWorks: You answer a call and hear a prerecorded message, sometimes from a voice like "Susie" with a "Vehicle Service Department," claiming they've sent several notices about your vehicle's manufacturer warranty and that your file will be closed soon unless you respond. The recording tells you to press one number to renew the "warranty" or another to be removed from the call list. In reality, the companies behind these calls have no relationship with your car dealer or manufacturer. The "extended warranty" being pitched is actually a service contract that can sell for hundreds or thousands of dollars, and fine-print restrictions often mean it won't actually cover problems with your car.
redFlags: Prerecorded robocall claiming your vehicle's factory warranty is about to expire or has already lapsed
Caller claims to be from a generic "Vehicle Service Department" rather than your actual dealer or manufacturer
Pressure to press a number immediately to renew coverage before your "file" is closed
Being asked to buy a costly service contract over an unsolicited call rather than through your dealer
realExamples: FTC consumer alert describing a recorded message from a caller claiming to be "Susie" with the "Vehicle Service Department" warning that a vehicle's manufacturer warranty was about to expire
reports.source: FTC, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2021/05/hang-auto-warranty-robocalls

reports.title: Phantom Debt Collector Scam
reports.summary: Scammers posing as debt collectors or law firms call or mail consumers demanding payment on debts that don't exist, threatening arrest, lawsuits, wage garnishment, or ruined credit if they don't pay immediately.
safetyTips: Ask for a written validation notice and the collector's name, company, address, and license to collect debts in your state before discussing anything
Never pay a debt you can't verify; check your own account records and credit report first
Remember that a real debt collector will never threaten immediate arrest or jail time for an unpaid debt
Hang up and independently look up the supposed company or law firm's official phone number rather than calling back a number the caller gave you
Report suspected phantom debt collectors to your state attorney general and the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters operate under invented or borrowed company and law-firm names and contact consumers by phone, letter, text, email, or social media claiming they owe an old payday loan, credit card balance, or other debt. The callers falsely claim to be lawyers or process servers, even though they have no legal authority to collect anything, and pressure victims with threats of lawsuits, wage garnishment, damaged credit, and even arrest if they don't pay right away, usually demanding payment by phone with a card or other untraceable method. In one FTC case, a scheme operated under names like Blackrock Services, Blackstone Legal Group, Capital Legal Services, Quest Legal Group, and Viking Legal Services, sending deceptive collection letters and calls claiming consumers owed money on a payday loan and that a "law firm" was about to sue them, when the debts never existed at all. The operators also violate the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act by never sending the legally required written validation notice and by failing to disclose that they are debt collectors.
redFlags: Caller claims to be a lawyer or law firm but won't provide a callable business address or license information
You never receive a written validation notice within five days of being contacted, which real debt collectors are legally required to send
The caller demands immediate payment by phone, prepaid card, wire transfer, or other untraceable method
Threats of immediate arrest, jail time, or wage garnishment over an unfamiliar or very old debt
The company name is unfamiliar, slightly altered from a real business, or you cannot verify it independently
Pressure to pay before you can check your own records or credit report for the debt
realExamples: FTC lawsuit and March 2025 federal court order halted a phantom debt collection scheme run under names including Blackrock Services, Blackstone Legal Group, Capital Legal Services, Quest Legal Group, and Viking Legal Services, which sent fictitious debt collection notices and calls nationwide threatening lawsuits, wage garnishment, credit damage, and arrest over debts that never existed

The FTC filed suit against Global Asset Financial Services Group (GAFS) and fifteen related defendants whose employees falsely claimed to be lawyers or affiliated with law firms despite having no authority to collect debts

An earlier FTC case against a Charlotte, NC debt collection operation found the 'collectors' used various law-firm-sounding names and threatened people with arrest, jail time, or lawsuits over payday loans or other debts unless they paid immediately by credit or debit card
reports.source: FTC, https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/03/ftc-action-leads-court-order-halting-phantom-debt-collection-scheme-took-millions-consumers

reports.title: Rogue Mover "Hostage Load" Scam
reports.summary: Dishonest interstate moving companies lure customers with a low, non-binding estimate, then load the customer's entire household onto the truck and refuse to deliver or unload it until an inflated payment is made.
safetyTips: Get a written estimate based on an actual in-home inventory walk-through before booking
Verify the company's registration and complaint history through FMCSA's online resources before booking
Review FMCSA's moving fraud prevention checklist and tips for a successful move before your move
If you experience moving fraud, file a complaint with FMCSA's national consumer complaint database or call the nationwide complaint hotline
reports.howItWorks: A "rogue mover" or unregistered broker gives a customer a low estimate without ever doing an in-home survey, and may ask the customer to sign incomplete documents. On moving day, the crew loads every box and piece of furniture onto the truck, then presents a dramatically higher bill — far above the original quote. Because the goods are already loaded, the company holds the shipment "hostage," refusing to unload or deliver it until the customer pays the new, inflated amount. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), the DOT agency that enforces federal consumer protection regulations related to the interstate shipment of household goods, has run enforcement campaigns against such movers and brokers.
redFlags: No in-home estimate before giving a quote
Mover asks you to sign incomplete documentation
Company fails to register with FMCSA
realExamples: FMCSA's newsroom describes a nationwide enforcement sweep "ahead of busy summer moving season" in which the agency conducted an enforcement sweep and provided consumer resources after complaints about movers holding possessions hostage.

FMCSA's 2013 "Protect Your Move" campaign announcement noted that among the most common complaints in 2012 were shipments being held hostage, loss, damage or delay of shipments, unauthorized movers, and deceptive practices such as overcharges, with New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago topping the list of cities with the most complaints that year.
reports.source: FMCSA, https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/newsroom/fmcsa-continues-nationwide-crackdown-fraudulent-household-goods-movers-and-brokers and https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/newsroom/us-department-transportation-launches-protect-your-move-campaign-help-consumers-spot-red

reports.title: Fake Check Scam Targeting Childcare Providers
reports.summary: Scammers pose as parents urgently needing childcare, send providers a check for more than owed, then ask for the "overpayment" to be wired or sent back — leaving the provider on the hook when the check bounces.
safetyTips: Take your time before engaging with someone who contacts you urgently, especially if you haven't worked with or met them before
Don't accept a check for more than you charge for childcare — that's a sure sign of a scam
Never send money back to anyone who says they overpaid you by check; only a scammer asks you to repay an overpayment via wire, payment app, gift cards, or crypto
Remember that a check can look legitimate and funds can appear in your account, but the check can still bounce days later, leaving you liable for the full amount
reports.howItWorks: Scammers posing as parents contact childcare providers by email, text, social media, or online caregiving platforms, claiming they are moving to the area, often from overseas, and need immediate childcare. They send a check to pay for services in advance, but the check is written for more than the agreed amount. The "parent" then explains they "accidentally overpaid" and asks the provider to send the extra money back, usually by wire transfer or payment app. The provider deposits the check, sees the funds appear, and sends back the difference — but the check later bounces, leaving the provider responsible for repaying their bank the full amount, while the money they sent to the scammer is gone for good.
redFlags: An unfamiliar "parent" reaches out urgently needing childcare, often claiming to be moving from overseas
You receive a check for more money than you were owed for your services
The sender asks you to send back the "overpaid" amount via wire transfer, payment app, gift cards, or cryptocurrency
Contact comes out of the blue via email, text, social media, or a caregiving platform before you've even met
realExamples: Childcare providers have reported scammers posing as parents moving to the area from overseas who send a check for more than the arranged cost of care and ask for the difference to be wired back or sent via payment app.
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/05/fake-check-scam-targets-childcare-providers

reports.title: Blessing Loom / Circle Game Chain Letter Scam
reports.summary: A social-media "game" — also called the Blessing Loom, Mandala Game, Infinity Loom, or Money Board — tricks people into paying $100 to join an octagon-shaped payment pyramid, promising an $800 payout that almost never arrives.
safetyTips: Treat any 'game,' 'loom,' or 'board' that asks you to pay to join and recruit others as an illegal pyramid scheme, not a real investment
Don't send money through PayPal or other payment apps to strangers or acquaintances to join an online recruitment game
If a friend or family member invites you to join, warn them it's a scam instead of participating
Remember that in chain-letter pyramid schemes nearly everyone loses money except those at the very top who got in first
Report it to the FTC at ftc.gov/complaint if you're invited to join or if you've already lost money
reports.howItWorks: Scammers recruit through posts or direct messages on Instagram, Facebook, and other social media inviting people to join a "Circle," "Loom," or "Board." To join, a person sends $100 through PayPal or another digital payment app to whoever occupies the center of an octagon-shaped graphic, which secures them a spot on the outer ring. As more people pay to join, the board splits and expands, and players are told they can move toward the center by recruiting new people themselves. Once a player's name finally reaches the center, they are supposed to collect $100 each from eight new recruits on the outer ring before leaving the game or starting over. No product or service is sold and no real investment generates the payouts — the only money coming in is from new recruits, so once people run out of friends or strangers to recruit, the money dries up and everyone still waiting at the outer rings loses what they paid.
redFlags: Invitation arrives as a social media post or DM urging you to join a 'game,' 'circle,' 'loom,' or 'board'
You're asked to pay another private individual directly via PayPal or a digital payment app to secure a spot
The pitch promises a fixed large payout (e.g., $800) for a small upfront payment (e.g., $100) with no product or service involved
Payouts depend entirely on recruiting new participants rather than any real investment or business activity
Friends or family who've already joined pressure you to sign up too
realExamples: FTC consumer alert describes the scheme circulating under names like 'The Circle Game,' 'Blessing Loom,' and 'Money Board,' spreading at a time when many people were out of work and looking for extra cash
Commenters on the FTC's alert page describe joining after a friend or family member recruited them, paying in along with a relative, and never receiving the promised payout
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2020/05/game-chain-letter-scam

reports.title: Government Grant Scam
reports.summary: Scammers claim you've been approved for a "free" government grant to pay bills, home repairs, or education costs, then steal your personal information or demand upfront fees paid in untraceable ways.
relatedScams: Fake Social Security Statement Email Scam
safetyTips: Never share your Social Security number, bank account, or card details with anyone who contacts you about a grant
Remember that real government agencies won't call, text, email, or message you on social media to offer free grants
Know that the only official source for federal grant listings is grants.gov, and applying is always free
If you already paid, contact the gift card issuer, money transfer company, or crypto platform immediately to try to reverse the transaction
Report suspected grant scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: A scammer reaches out unsolicited — by phone, text, email, or social media/chat app — claiming you qualify for a free government grant to cover personal expenses like bills, home repairs, medical costs, or education. They first ask for personal information such as your Social Security number to see if you "qualify" (you always will), then ask for your bank account information, supposedly to direct-deposit the grant, or demand you pay "processing" or other fees via gift card, cash reload card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency. Some versions impersonate a real agency like the Social Security Administration or use an official-sounding fake name like the "Federal Grants Administration," which doesn't actually exist. Once the scammer has the bank details or fee payment, the money disappears and no grant ever materializes.
redFlags: Being contacted out of the blue about a government grant you never applied for
Being asked to pay any upfront 'processing' or other fee to receive grant money
Requests to pay via gift card, cash reload card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency
Promises that you're guaranteed to qualify or that you'll get a refund if unsatisfied
Contact via phone, text, email, or social media claiming to be from a government agency
realExamples: Scammers pretend to be with a real government agency like the Social Security Administration, or make up an official-sounding name like the 'Federal Grants Administration,' to convince people they qualify for free government grant money before asking for personal information, bank details, or upfront fees paid by gift card, cash reload card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency.
reports.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Government Grant Scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/government-grant-scams

reports.title: Fake USPTO "Trademark Verification Appointment" Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send official-looking emails impersonating the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, demanding trademark applicants call an "examining attorney" for a mandatory verification appointment or risk losing their trademark.
relatedScams: FTC Impersonator Fake Employee ID Refund Recovery Scam
safetyTips: Never call phone numbers listed in unsolicited trademark-related emails; verify application status directly through the USPTO's official TSDR system at tsdr.uspto.gov
Remember that genuine USPTO communications about your application come in writing via Office Actions filed through TEAS, generally allowing three to six months to respond, not urgent phone deadlines
If you work with a trademark attorney, have official correspondence routed through their office so you don't have to judge on your own whether an email is real
Check the sender's full email domain carefully rather than just the display name, since scammers spoof official-sounding addresses
Report suspicious USPTO impersonation emails to the USPTO and file a complaint with the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov rather than replying or calling the number provided
reports.howItWorks: Because nearly all trademark application data (owner name, serial number, legal entity type, address, and assigned USPTO law office) is publicly searchable in the USPTO's Trademark Status and Document Retrieval database, scammers scrape this real information and mail-merge it into convincing phishing emails. The emails use urgent subject lines and claim the applicant must schedule or attend a "mandatory verification appointment" with a supposed examining attorney, warning that failure to do so could result in abandonment of the application. Victims who call the listed phone number may be asked by the scammer to provide payment information, personal identifying information, or both, which can then be used for fraud. The senders use look-alike domains rather than the real @uspto.gov address to make the messages appear legitimate.
redFlags: Email demands a "mandatory verification appointment" or phone call with an "examining attorney" " the USPTO does not schedule such calls
Sender domain is not @uspto.gov (reported lookalikes include domains such as @uspto-trademark.live, @lawoffice119.com, and @uspto-trademark-gov.live)
Message threatens abandonment of the trademark application if you don't call by a specific date/time
Caller or email attempts to obtain payment information or personal identifying information over the phone
Urgent, all-caps subject lines like "ACTION REQUIRED: MANDATORY VERIFICATION APPOINTMENT"
realExamples: Law firms and trademark applicants reported receiving fraudulent emails impersonating the USPTO with subject lines like "ACTION REQUIRED: MANDATORY VERIFICATION APPOINTMENT" and "OFFICIAL NOTICE OF TRADEMARK VERIFICATION APPOINTMENT," citing real application details such as serial number, entity type, address, and assigned law office, and sent from domains such as @uspto-trademark.live rather than @uspto.gov.
reports.source: Stites & Harbison PLLC, https://www.stites.com/resources/client-alerts/trademark-applicants-beware-the-latest-uspto-impersonation-scam-using-fake-verification-appointments/

reports.title: Boss/CEO Gift Card Impersonation (BEC) Scam
reports.summary: Scammers impersonate a company executive or boss via spoofed email, text, or phone call, urgently asking an employee to buy gift cards and send back the codes. It's one of the most common and persistent forms of Business Email Compromise (BEC) fraud.
safetyTips: Never purchase gift cards based solely on an email or text request, no matter how urgent it sounds or who it appears to be from
Verify any unusual request by contacting the supposed sender directly through a known phone number or in person, not by replying to the message or calling a number it provides
Watch for mismatched or spoofed email domains and report suspicious messages to your IT or security team
Remember that legitimate executives, businesses, and government agencies never ask employees or customers to pay via gift card codes
Report incidents to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3.gov) so patterns can be tracked and investigated
reports.howItWorks: A criminal researches a company's leadership on sites like LinkedIn or the corporate website, then impersonates a CEO, HR director, or other authority figure by spoofing their email address or phone number (sometimes buying breached credentials and contact lists to make the impersonation more convincing). The fake "boss" contacts an employee claiming to be in meetings or traveling and unable to talk, and asks for an urgent "favor": purchasing gift cards (Apple, Google Play, Target, etc.) for clients, staff gifts, or a client reimbursement. The message pressures the employee to act fast and keep it confidential. Once the employee buys the cards, the scammer instructs them to scratch off the back and photograph or text the card numbers and PINs, at which point the funds are cashed out within minutes and the "boss" goes silent.
redFlags: Urgent, time-pressured request from a 'boss' or executive asking you to buy gift cards
Sender claims to be unreachable by phone because they are 'in a meeting' and asks you to just reply to email or text
Request to send back gift card numbers and PINs (or photos of the scratched-off codes) rather than the physical cards
Email address or phone number that looks almost identical to the real supervisor's but has a subtle difference (e.g., a swapped letter or different domain)
Instructions to keep the purchase secret or not mention it to coworkers
realExamples: The FBI's Phoenix field office issued a Tech Tuesday bulletin describing BEC scams where a spoofed email or text from a 'CEO or HR director' tells an employee to purchase gift cards for the executive to give away or use for a party, with the employee told to send back the card number and PIN.

A cybersecurity write-up citing a January 2026 FBI consumer alert titled about bosses asking for gift cards noted that gift card requests are now a common BEC variant, including text requests sent to employees' personal phones, often relying on data harvested from breached accounts to impersonate executives convincingly.

Proofpoint research found that since March 2020, over 7,000 CEOs or other executives have been impersonated in these schemes, with a single CEO on average impersonated 102 times across a 90-day period.
An industry analysis reported that gift card schemes represented 37.9% of all BEC incidents in Q1 2024, calling them the top BEC cash-out method.
reports.source: FBI Phoenix Field Office, https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/phoenix/news/press-releases/fbi-tech-tuesday-business-email-compromise-bec-gift-card-fraud

reports.title: Solar / Clean Energy Home Improvement Scam
reports.summary: Scammers posing as government officials or utility company reps push "free" solar panels and energy-efficiency upgrades, then stick homeowners with hidden costs, predatory financing, or no installation at all.
safetyTips: Know that 'free' or 'no cost' solar panel offers are always scams \u2014 check the Department of Energy's or Department of Treasury's official guidance before considering solar
Take your time; anyone who pressures you into a contract or demands up-front or immediate payment is a scammer
Legitimate businesses and government agencies don't pressure you to act immediately and won't ask you to pay with cash, gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps, or cryptocurrency
Protect your personal information; don't respond to unexpected requests online or on social media for your name, address, or other personal information to 'see if you qualify'
Report solar and clean energy imposters to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: The scam usually starts with an unexpected phone call, a social media message, or an in-person visit from someone claiming to represent the government or the homeowner's utility company. The so-called official offers a "free" energy audit or tries to sign the homeowner up for a program to make their home more energy efficient with solar panels, falsely claiming the utility company already enrolled them and now they just need to pay. The pitch typically includes promises of big savings on utility bills, free or low-cost solar panels, or huge rebates, tax credits, or utility incentives covering the cost — all of which are lies, since the federal government does not install solar systems in homes for free. Victims who agree can end up locked into unfair financing schemes or predatory contracts that cost tens of thousands of dollars.
redFlags: Claims to be from the government or your utility company offering 'free' or 'no cost' solar panels
High-pressure tactics demanding you sign a contract or pay immediately
Says your utility company already signed you up for a solar program and now you owe money
Requests payment by cash, gift card, wire transfer, payment app, or cryptocurrency
realExamples: FTC Consumer Alert describes scammers calling, messaging on social media, or visiting in person claiming to be from the government or a utility, offering a 'free' energy audit or solar sign-up program and claiming the utility already enrolled the homeowner
reports.source: FTC Consumer Alerts, "How to avoid getting burned by solar or clean energy scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/08/how-avoid-getting-burned-solar-or-clean-energy-scams

reports.title: TikTok "VIP Upgrade" Crypto Inheritance DM Scam
reports.summary: A brand-new TikTok account DMs strangers a melodramatic "last goodbye" story claiming to have left them crypto assets, then lures them to a fake exchange site showing a huge balance that can never actually be withdrawn without paying escalating "VIP upgrade" fees.
safetyTips: Never pay a fee to 'unlock' or withdraw money that is supposedly already yours \u2014 legitimate platforms do not charge you to access your own funds
Don't log into any crypto site or wallet using credentials someone else sent you in a DM
Treat any unsolicited inheritance, gift, or 'last goodbye' message on social media as a scam, especially from brand-new accounts
Verify any crypto balance independently on a public blockchain explorer rather than trusting an in-app dashboard
Report and block the account, and avoid providing personal details like your name, email, or phone number through the chat funnel
reports.howItWorks: The scam starts with a cold DM or comment from a newly created TikTok account telling a sob story — terminal illness, a "last goodbye," or a claim that the sender has left the recipient crypto assets — along with a ready-made username and password for a crypto site the victim has never used. Logging in reveals a large, legitimate-looking balance and a withdraw button, but any attempt to move the funds out triggers a demand for a "withdrawal key" supposedly belonging to the original account holder, which the victim doesn't have and support won't provide. Support then steers victims toward an "Internal Transfer" option and offers to help them create a new account "in seconds" that supposedly has its own key, making the next step feel legitimate; from there, victims are told they must pay to "upgrade" to VIP or membership tiers — reported amounts escalate from around 50 USDT at entry level up to 1,000, 3,000, and as much as 50,000 USDT for "full functionality" — purportedly to unlock the ability to transfer or withdraw the trapped funds. The displayed balance and all "proof" of funds exist only inside the scammer's own dashboard, with no public blockchain ledger ever confirming it, and the whole funnel is optimized for mobile, using large tap targets and persistent chat bubbles to keep victims moving quickly without stopping to verify.
redFlags: Unsolicited DM from a brand-new TikTok account with an emotional story (illness, death, 'last goodbye') offering you crypto assets
You're given someone else's login credentials to a crypto site you've never signed up for
A large balance appears instantly but withdrawals are blocked by a mysterious 'key' you don't possess
Support says you must buy a 'VIP' tier or membership to unlock withdrawals or internal transfers
No way to verify the funds exist outside the scammer's own dashboard (no public blockchain record, no small test withdrawal allowed)
Support uses free, informal email addresses rather than official corporate channels
realExamples: Malwarebytes documented TikTok DMs using a "terminal illness, last goodbye" story with a ready-made crypto site login, where any withdrawal attempt was blocked by a demand for a withdrawal key the victim never had.

Forbes reported on the same "VIP Membership Upgrade" scam, with a researcher explaining that victims see what looks like a real account with a large balance, but withdrawal attempts prompt a requirement for a key the scammer holds.
PhishFort's analysis described victims being asked to pay escalating 'upgrade' fees \u2014 from 50 USDT up to 50,000 USDT \u2014 to supposedly unlock a fabricated locked balance.
reports.source: Malwarebytes, https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2025/10/tiktok-scam-sells-you-access-to-your-own-fake-money ; Forbes, https://www.forbes.com/sites/daveywinder/2025/10/18/tiktok-users-warned-as-vip-upgrade-attack-strikes/ ; PhishFort, https://phishfort.com/vip-upgrade-crypto-scam/

reports.title: Impersonation Credit Repair Scheme (Fake Debt Collector/Creditor)
reports.summary: Scammers buy search ads that hijack people looking up real creditors or debt collectors, then pose as that company to charge illegal upfront "verification" fees and recurring charges for credit repair that never delivers.
safetyTips: Go directly to your creditor's or debt collector's official website or the number on your statement instead of clicking search ads or ad links
Remember that no company can legally remove accurate, timely negative information from your credit report
Never pay a credit repair company before it has completed the promised services — upfront fees are illegal under the Credit Repair Organizations Act
Report suspected credit repair scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: According to an FTC complaint, a credit repair network operated under the name Credit Glory and more than a dozen related company names, running since at least 2016. The operation bought paid Google search ads that appeared when consumers searched for specific creditors or debt collectors, including military-related lenders, and used those ads to route consumers to its own telemarketers instead of the real company. Once on the phone, the telemarketers let consumers believe they had reached the actual creditor or debt collector, then charged a fee — often described as needed to "verify" the consumer's identity — before signing people up for recurring subscription charges for credit repair services that falsely promised to remove negative information and boost credit scores. The FTC alleges this violated the Credit Repair Organizations Act, which bars charging consumers before credit repair work is completed.
redFlags: A company you find through a search ad claims to be your existing creditor or debt collector
You're asked to pay a fee before any credit repair work is done, sometimes framed as an 'identity verification' charge
Promises to remove all negative information from your credit report, even if it's accurate
Automatic recurring monthly charges you didn't clearly agree to
No detailed written contract explaining services, costs, and your cancellation rights before you pay
realExamples: FTC complaint alleges Credit Glory, a network of 16 related entities and five principals, scammed consumers out of nearly $200 million through unlawful up-front and recurring charges since at least 2016.

The FTC's complaint notes the defendants used paid search advertising to specifically target military servicemembers owing debts to military-related creditors such as Army & Air Force Exchange Service and USAA, falsely promising to improve their credit.
reports.source: FTC, "FTC Stops Sprawling Credit Repair Scheme that Scammed Consumers Out of Nearly $200 Million," https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/08/ftc-stops-sprawling-credit-repair-scheme-scammed-consumers-out-nearly-200-million

reports.title: Fake Flight Cancellation Text Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send travelers a text that looks like an official airline alert saying their flight was canceled or delayed, pushing them to call a fake "rebooking" number or click a link that steals money and personal data.
safetyTips: Never call a number or click a link provided in an unsolicited flight cancellation text; instead verify status directly through the airline's official app or website
Use only the customer service number listed in your booking confirmation, the airline's app, or its verified website, not one sent via text or social media message
Be suspicious of any 'representative' who asks for a rebooking fee, gift card numbers, wire transfers, or your bank login
Slow down when a message uses high-pressure language like 'call now' or 'act fast'; take a minute to verify independently before responding
Report suspicious messages by forwarding scam texts to 7726 (SPAM) and reporting fake airline messages to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: The scam starts with a text message that appears to come from a real airline and includes personal touches like the traveler's name and actual flight number, along with urgent wording claiming the flight has been canceled or delayed and instructing the recipient to "call this number" or "click to rebook." Travelers who call reach a scammer posing as an airline representative who offers to rebook the flight for a fee and may ask for payment details or personal information like a birth date or passport number, sometimes sending official-looking confirmation emails to make the lie more believable, while those who click the link are sent to a phishing page designed to harvest payment and personal information. Many scammers now use AI tools to generate convincing language and fake confirmations that mimic real airline alerts, making these messages harder to spot, and they often arrive during busy travel seasons or storm delays when victims are primed to believe a cancellation notice.
redFlags: Unsolicited text claiming your specific flight is canceled or delayed with a 'call this number' or 'click to rebook' link
Urgent, pressure-filled language like 'act fast' or 'your seat will be canceled' meant to rush you into responding
A phone number in the text differs from the one on your actual booking confirmation, the airline's app, or its verified website
Request for a rebooking fee or payment card details, or personal information like your birth date or passport number, over the phone
Message arrives during busy travel seasons or storm delays, a tactic scammers use to seem more credible
realExamples: Fox News/CyberGuy reported scammers sending texts with the recipient's name and real flight number, telling them to 'call this number' or 'click to rebook' after claiming a flight was canceled or delayed
The Better Business Bureau reported a surge in fake cancellation notices that include phony phone numbers leading straight to scammers
reports.source: Fox News/CyberGuy, https://www.foxnews.com/tech/fake-flight-cancellation-texts-target-travelers

reports.title: Homework Helper / Test Prep Extortion Scam
reports.summary: Students who pay online "tutoring" or test-prep companies to do their homework or exams for them find the company later demands more money and threatens to expose them to their school for cheating if they don't pay up.
safetyTips: Never pay someone to complete your own assignments or take exams for you; this is cheating and creates blackmail leverage
Get tutoring referrals from friends, family, teachers, or honor society tutoring programs instead of unknown online companies
Check references for any tutoring service and speak with at least three past clients before paying
Agree on availability, rates, and scope of services in writing up front to avoid surprise fees
Report extortion attempts to BBB Scam Tracker rather than paying the demanded money
reports.howItWorks: A student struggling in a class searches online for a tutoring company that offers to actually complete assignments or exams rather than teach the material, and pays upfront, often a couple hundred dollars, for help with coursework such as math or technology classes. After payment, instead of delivering the promised help, the company demands additional money, inventing excuses like extra "research" fees. If the student refuses to keep paying, the scammers turn to extortion, sending threatening emails or texts claiming they will report the student to their college or university as a cheater using the assignments and message history as "evidence," pushing frightened students to pay thousands of dollars to protect their academic standing.
redFlags: A company offers to complete your homework or exams for you rather than help you learn the material
You're asked to sign a disclaimer or waiver before work begins, which is later used against you
Requests for extra, unexplained fees after the initial payment (e.g., for "additional research")
Threats to report you to your school or have you expelled if you stop paying or ask for a refund
realExamples: BBB Scam Tracker received a report describing a company that had students sign a disclaimer, then used that document and chat messages to threaten to tell their college to get them expelled
Another victim reported that when they asked for a refund, the company threatened to email their school or teacher claiming the student had cheated
reports.source: Better Business Bureau, https://www.bbb.org/article/news-releases/24032-bbb-scam-alert-students-hire-homework-help-and-end-up-in-extortion-con

reports.title: Fake Process Server Phishing Call Scam
reports.summary: Scammers call claiming to be a "process server" with an urgent, non-existent lawsuit, lien, or warrant against you or a family member, then pressure you to "confirm" your Social Security number and other personal details.
safetyTips: Never confirm or give out your Social Security number, date of birth, or other personal details to an unsolicited caller
Check your local court's website to see if a lawsuit has actually been filed against you or a family member
Be wary of scare tactics and unsolicited phone calls; representatives of a reputable business or legal office will be polite and civil and won't pressure you to act immediately
Don't give out personal information about family members either; if someone asks you to validate information about another individual, hang up the phone
Report the call to the BBB Scam Tracker so others can be warned
reports.howItWorks: You get a call, sometimes repeated, from an unknown or blocked number from someone claiming to be a process server. They might say there is a lien on your home or that you're being taken to court over unpaid medical bills or another debt, or claim you or a family member are a "person of interest in an important matter" and that federal law prevents them from sharing more details until papers are served. The caller then asks you to "confirm" sensitive personal information such as your date of birth, address, or Social Security number, stressing urgency when you hesitate. If you push back and ask who is filing the complaint or what company the caller works for, the scammer often gets angry and threatens arrest or further legal action. In some versions the scammer already has partial personal information about a targeted family member, which they use to make the threat seem credible, or they call relatives of the target to demand the relatives contact the consumer and have them call the scammer back.
redFlags: Caller ID is unknown or blocked and the caller claims to be a process server
Caller refuses to identify the company they work for or who filed the complaint, citing 'federal law' as the reason
You're pressured to 'confirm' your Social Security number, date of birth, or address over the phone
The caller reacts with anger or threats of arrest when you ask clarifying questions
Claims of a lien, lawsuit, or warrant that you cannot verify on your local court's website
realExamples: A BBB Scam Tracker report described a caller who said they were a process server with papers regarding a lien on a consumer's home, which turned out to be false after checking with the police department and town.

Another consumer reported a caller identifying as 'Roy Smith' who demanded SSN verification, threatened arrest when refused, and then called the consumer's son and a friend, threatening them with arrest if they did not contact the consumer and have them call back.

A reported voicemail claimed to be from 'Independent Process Service dispatch division' saying a parent owed medical bills and that papers would be served at home or work, directing the family to call back a given number and reference code.
reports.source: Better Business Bureau, https://www.bbb.org/article/scams/28919-bbb-scam-alert-this-phishing-scam-claims-a-process-server-is-looking-for-you

reports.title: Fake "Shop to Support" Animal Shelter TikTok Charity Scam
reports.summary: Scammers post heartstring-tugging TikTok and social media videos of "elderly" shelter owners making handmade pet products to save a failing animal shelter, then pocket the money when shoppers buy the never-delivered merchandise.
safetyTips: Don't give in to videos that tug at your heartstrings or create a sense of urgency, even if you're excited about the product
Check to see if the charity is real on Give.org before purchasing or donating
Look up the company name, website, and contact information, read reviews on bbb.org, and search the company's name with the word "scam" before buying
Only do business with companies you know and trust, or research unfamiliar companies thoroughly first
Give locally by contacting your local or state animal shelters or other agencies directly to ask how you can support them
reports.howItWorks: While scrolling TikTok or another social platform, a user sees a video of an older adult asking for help, often showing cats or other animals in a shelter along with captions claiming the person is struggling to keep their shelter open and is making products like cat toys or slippers to fund it. The video shows craft-store footage and a finished product, uses emotional music and urgent captions, and includes a link in the description directing viewers to a website to buy the item "to support the cause." Shoppers who order the merchandise never receive anything, and it is unclear whether any money actually goes to a real charity; BBB has found the accompanying videos, photos, and backstories are frequently AI-generated or stolen from other accounts rather than depicting a real shelter or person.
redFlags: Videos use urgent emotional pleas like "please stay for 8 seconds to help my cat shelter from shutting down" or "please don't scroll for 12 seconds to help my failing animal shelter"
The featured charity or shelter has no verifiable information, address, or nonprofit status anywhere online
Heavy use of touching music, cute animals, and elderly people designed to trigger sympathy and impulse purchases
A purchase link leads to a standalone sales website rather than a verified charity donation page
Videos and product stories appear reused across multiple accounts selling different items (cat toys, cow slippers, etc.)
realExamples: BBB Scam Tracker received a report describing a TikTok account called FlappyBirdUS showing "a little old man and his wife who 'make cat toys to support their failing cat shelter'" that led to a site called meowwings.com where buyers paid but received nothing and could find no real information about the shelter, with the same fake, AI-generated videos recycled under other accounts selling cow slippers instead.
reports.source: Better Business Bureau (BBB Scam Tracker / BBB of Eastern Carolinas) - https://www.bbb.org/scamtracker/lookupscam/992747 and https://lakeoconeebreeze.net/2025/06/20/bbb-scam-alert-tiktok-videos-use-sad-stories-in-fake-donation-request/

reports.title: Mail Theft Check Washing/Check Cooking Scam
reports.summary: Criminals steal checks straight out of mailboxes or USPS collection boxes, then chemically "wash" or digitally "cook" them to change the payee and amount before cashing them, often before the victim even notices the check is missing.
relatedScams: Fake Check Scam Targeting Childcare Providers
safetyTips: Avoid mailing checks when possible; use online bill pay, electronic transfers, or hand checks directly to a postal worker or drop them inside the post office rather than in a mailbox or collection box
Write checks in black gel ink, which is more resistant to chemical washing than ballpoint pen
Regularly monitor bank statements and set up account alerts to catch unauthorized transactions quickly
Pick up mail promptly and do not leave outgoing mail in a mailbox overnight or for long periods
Report suspected mail theft or check fraud immediately to your bank, local police, and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters obtain legitimate, signed checks by stealing them from residential mailboxes, USPS blue collection boxes after the last pickup, or through burglary, robbery, or bribery of postal facilities/employees. Once they have a check, they either "wash" it using chemicals to erase the original ink and rewrite the payee and dollar amount, or they "cook" it by digitally editing a photographed image of the check with photo-editing software and high-end printers, which lets them manufacture multiple counterfeit checks — often in smaller amounts — from a single stolen check image. Unaltered stolen checks are sometimes deposited directly using forged endorsements. Because banking regulations require funds from deposited checks to be made available to the depositor within a short window, the forged or altered checks often clear and the money is withdrawn by the criminals before the fraud is detected by the bank, the original account holder, or law enforcement.
redFlags: Unfamiliar transactions or a check cleared for a different amount or payee than you wrote appear on your bank statement
Your bank calls about a check or withdrawal you don't recognize
A check you mailed was never received by the intended recipient, or took unusually long to clear
You notice your residential mailbox or a nearby USPS collection box has been tampered with
Someone unexpectedly asks you to deposit and forward funds from a check you received
realExamples: The FBI and USPIS issued a January 2025 public service announcement warning that check fraud is on the rise, with Suspicious Activity Reports related to check fraud nearly doubling from 2021 to 2023

The PSA described five methods criminals use to obtain checks: theft from residential mailboxes left overnight, theft from USPS blue collection boxes after last pickup, burglary of USPS facilities, robbery of USPS employees, and bribery/collusion with postal employees
Officials noted fraudsters also use spoofing technology and AI-assisted voice recreation to trick vulnerable people into becoming unwitting accomplices in moving the stolen funds
reports.source: FBI/IC3 Public Service Announcement, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250127

reports.title: Senior U.S. Official Impersonation Messaging Scam
reports.summary: Malicious actors send AI-generated text and voice messages pretending to be senior U.S. government officials, build rapport with the target, then move the conversation to an encrypted app to steal account access, personal documents, or funds.
safetyTips: Do not assume a message is authentic just because it claims to be from a current or former senior U.S. official
Independently look up and call a verified phone number for the person or agency rather than using contact info provided in the message
Carefully examine the phone number, email address, and spelling used in the message for inconsistencies
Never share authentication codes, PII, or financial information over text or encrypted messaging apps
Report suspicious messages to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) and preserve the messages as evidence
reports.howItWorks: According to the FBI, since at least 2023 malicious actors have used smishing (fake texts) and vishing (AI-generated voice messages) that claim to come from senior U.S. state government, White House, or Cabinet-level officials, as well as members of Congress, to target officials' family members, personal acquaintances, and other contacts. The actor opens with a text, briefly engages the victim on a topic they're knowledgeable about (current events, trade or security policy, bilateral relations) to build rapport, and almost immediately asks to move the conversation to an encrypted messaging app such as Signal, Telegram, or WhatsApp. Once trust is established, the impersonator may request a wire transfer, propose a meeting with "high-ranking officials," note a fake appointment to company leadership, request copies of personal documents, or simply ask about U.S. policy. Gaining access to a victim's personal or official accounts lets the actor pivot to target that person's own contacts and associates using the trusted relationship, or use the harvested contact information to impersonate others and elicit more information or funds.
redFlags: Unsolicited text or AI-generated voice message claiming to be from a senior government official, sometimes with poor grammar or unusual phrasing
Message quickly tries to shift the conversation from SMS to an encrypted app like Signal, Telegram, or WhatsApp
Sender references current events or policy topics to build rapport before making any request
Requests for a wire transfer, personal documents, authentication codes, or other sensitive information
Promise of a meeting with other high-ranking officials or a fake leadership appointment
realExamples: FBI IC3 PSA I-051525-PSA (May 15, 2025) warned that since April 2025 malicious actors had impersonated senior U.S. officials using smishing and AI-generated vishing to target current and former government officials and their contacts

FBI IC3 PSA I-121925-PSA (December 19, 2025) updated the alert, noting activity dating back to 2023 involving impersonation of senior state government, White House, Cabinet-level officials, and members of Congress

The U.S. State Department Office of Inspector General issued a fraud alert describing actors texting Department personnel while posing as the Inspector General or other senior officials and pushing them to continue the conversation on Signal, Telegram, or WhatsApp
reports.source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251219

reports.title: FCC Commissioner Impersonation "Phone Number Under Investigation" Scam
reports.summary: Scammers are posing as Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Commissioners or employees in calls, texts, and emails, falsely claiming a victim's phone number is linked to criminal activity in order to extract payment or personal financial information.
safetyTips: Know that the FCC will never ask you for payment of any kind over the phone, including cash apps, cryptocurrency, gift cards, or store credit
Know that the FCC will never ask for your Social Security number, driver's license number, bank account information, or security information like PINs and passwords
Do not respond if you think you've been contacted by phone, text, or email by an FCC or government imposter, and hang up immediately if it's a call
Talk to someone you trust if you're worried about a problem with your account or identity, especially if the stranger claims to be from the government
Report FCC imposter scams using the FCC's online complaint form
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters contact consumers by phone, text message, or email pretending to be an FCC Commissioner or agency staff member, sometimes using the names of actual FCC employees to make the call seem more convincing. The impostors falsely claim that the consumer's phone number is under investigation for criminal activity. They then demand immediate payment or request personal and financial information to supposedly resolve the issue, and may threaten to take action if the person doesn't comply. The FCC has confirmed it never asks for payment over the phone, never asks for personal or security information, and never threatens to take action if you don't give money or personal information.
redFlags: Caller or texter claims to be an FCC Commissioner or employee and says your phone number is under criminal investigation
Immediate demand for payment or personal/financial information over the phone or by text
Threats to take action if you don't comply with a request for money or personal information
Request for payment via cash apps, cryptocurrency, gift cards, or store credit
Caller uses the name of an actual FCC employee to seem more convincing
realExamples: Callers falsely claim that a consumer's phone number is under investigation for criminal activity, then demand immediate payment or personal financial information to resolve the supposed issue, sometimes using the names of actual FCC employees to make the scheme seem more convincing.
reports.source: FCC, "How to Spot FCC Imposters" consumer alert, https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/scam-alert/how-spot-fcc-imposters

reports.title: DEA/Medical Board License Revocation Impersonation Scam
reports.summary: Scammers posing as DEA agents or state licensing board staff call or mail letters to doctors, dentists, nurses, and other licensed professionals, falsely claiming their license is under investigation or about to be revoked unless they pay fees or hand over personal information.
relatedScams: Senior U.S. Official Impersonation Messaging Scam
safetyTips: Hang up and independently look up and call your licensing board or the DEA Diversion hotline directly rather than calling back a number given by the caller
Remember that real DEA agents and licensing boards do not call demanding immediate payment or threaten arrest/license loss over the phone
Never send payment via prepaid cards, wire transfer, cryptocurrency ATM, or gift cards to resolve a licensing or legal matter
Verify any letter or email by contacting your board through its official published phone number or website, not contact info included in the suspicious message
Report suspicious calls or letters to ic3.gov, reportfraud.ftc.gov, and your professional board's investigations division
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters call, email, or send fake letterhead mail to licensed practitioners claiming to be DEA agents or state medical/dental board investigators, reciting a fabricated badge number and alleging the victim's professional license is expiring, suspended, or was used in a crime. The FBI's September 2026 update to its law-enforcement impersonation warning notes that scammers may accuse medical practitioners of having an expiring medical license or claim their license was used in the commission of a crime, then threaten to revoke the practitioner's license, compelling the practitioner to pay to renew their license or protect their professional reputation
redFlags: Caller claims to be a DEA 'Officer' and opens by reciting a badge number before explaining the call
Demands for payment via prepaid cards, wire transfers, cash mailed or deposited into cryptocurrency ATMs/kiosks, or gift cards
Urgent, aggressive tone insisting you not tell colleagues, family, or your actual licensing board about the call
Threats to suspend or revoke a professional license unless you pay immediately or provide personal/financial information
Fake letters on official-looking board letterhead with forged signatures of real board executives
realExamples: The Mississippi State Board of Medical Licensure reported that several Mississippi physicians, including the board's own executive director, received voicemails from callers claiming to be DEA officers with fake badge numbers, alleging the physicians were under investigation for 'illegal activity' and threatening license suspension or revocation if they did not call back quickly.

The Mississippi board separately warned licensees about fraudulent letters on forged board letterhead, with a forged signature of the Executive Director, falsely notifying recipients that their medical license had been suspended due to federal criminal charges.

The FBI's nationwide PSA update reported that between January 2025 and July 2026 it received 3,322 IC3 complaints specifically for this license-threat variant of government impersonation fraud, with losses totaling more than $37 million.
reports.source: FBI/IC3 PSA (I-091726-PSA), https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260917 and Mississippi State Board of Medical Licensure, https://www.msbml.ms.gov/news/scam-alert-dea-impersonation-2026

reports.title: "Ghost Student" Financial Aid Fraud Scam
reports.summary: Organized fraud rings use stolen identities and AI-powered bots to enroll fake "ghost students" in online college courses, then collect and vanish with the federal and state financial aid money.
safetyTips: Create and regularly monitor your StudentAid.gov account, even if you have no plans to attend college, to check for unauthorized applications
Freeze your credit with the major bureaus to make it harder for fraudsters to use your Social Security number to open financial aid or loan accounts
Report suspected identity theft immediately to the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Education's Office of Inspector General

If you receive unexpected enrollment, transcript, or financial aid disbursement notices, contact the school's financial aid office directly using a verified phone number rather than any link in the notice
reports.howItWorks: Fraud rings start by harvesting stolen personal data such as names, Social Security numbers, and birthdates, often obtained through phishing attacks, healthcare breaches, or criminal marketplaces, and use it to build synthetic identities that can bypass basic verification steps in FAFSA applications and school enrollment portals. Once accepted, these identities are assigned real student accounts and financial aid packages, and automation/bots take over to submit FAFSA applications at scale, register for asynchronous or remote courses, generate human-sounding email replies, and create login activity that mimics real student behavior, since these schemes typically target online classes that require minimal in-person verification. The fake "student" enrolls in courses and files for federal or state financial aid; once the money is disbursed, the scammers vanish, leaving behind chaos for real students and the identity theft victims whose names were used. Victims often only discover the fraud when they try to apply for their own aid and find an account already exists in their name, or when they're contacted by loan servicers about debt they never took on.
redFlags: A FAFSA or StudentAid.gov account already exists under your name when you've never applied
Enrollment confirmations, transcript requests, or financial aid disbursement notices for a college you never attended
Courses with large numbers of enrolled students who never log in, submit coursework, or respond to outreach after the add/drop period
Unexplained student loan debt or aid disbursement discovered only when applying for your own benefits or via a loan servicer contact
realExamples: California's community college system reported that nearly a third of all student applications in 2024 were flagged as fraudulent, with ghost students siphoning off $5.6 million in federal student aid and $900,000 in state aid system-wide in just the first quarter of 2025
A Houston college graduate discovered a new FAFSA application had been filed in her name years after she had already graduated, after logging into her StudentAid.gov account
The U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issued an alert in consultation with other agencies about the growing ghost student fraud scheme
The U.S. Department of Education said it has prevented more than $1 billion in student aid fraud since January 2025, though the problem continues to accelerate
reports.source: Inside Higher Ed, https://www.insidehighered.com/news/institutions/community-colleges/2025/05/23/calif-community-colleges-ramp-battle-against-bots

reports.title: Foreclosure Relief / Mortgage Rescue Scam
reports.summary: Scammers target homeowners facing foreclosure with false promises of loan modification or "rescue" services, often posing as government-affiliated help while charging illegal upfront fees or stealing the title to the home.
safetyTips: Know that real government officials never ask for payment to help you with your mortgage
Remember companies offering mortgage assistance or foreclosure help cannot legally collect fees up front, only after a deal is reached
Contact your actual mortgage servicer or lender directly first before working with any third party
Never sign over the title or deed to your home to anyone other than your actual lender as part of a legitimate workout
Report suspected scams immediately since a foreclosure scam can cost you your home
reports.howItWorks: Companies and individuals target homeowners whose financial troubles put them at risk of losing their homes, frequently using mail or email designed to look like it's from a government agency. The CFPB warns that these outfits charge up-front fees (which is illegal for mortgage assistance), tell homeowners to stop making their mortgage payments, direct payments to someone other than the actual lender or servicer, pressure victims to sign over the title to their property in a so-called "rent to buy" scheme, push people to sign contracts they don't understand, claim to be conducting a "forensic audit" of the loan, and pressure victims to act immediately. Because the homeowner is already desperate and afraid of losing their home, they are especially vulnerable to pressure tactics and unfamiliar paperwork.
redFlags: Tells you to stop making mortgage payments
Demands an up-front fee before any help is provided
Asks you to send payments to someone other than your actual lender or servicer
Pressures you to sign over the title/deed to your home (a "rent to buy" scheme)
Claims to be doing a "forensic audit" of your loan
Pressures you to sign papers or contracts you don't understand or to act immediately
realExamples: A mortgage assistance or foreclosure relief scheme may charge up-front fees, tell a homeowner to stop making mortgage payments, direct payments to someone other than the lender or servicer, and pressure the homeowner to sign over the title to their property in a so-called "rent to buy" scheme.
reports.source: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/mortgages/how-to-spot-and-avoid-foreclosure-relief-scams/

reports.title: Fake Class Action Settlement Notice Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send fake emails and texts claiming you're owed money from a class-action lawsuit settlement, using the promise of a payout to steal personal data, bank details, or upfront "processing fees."
safetyTips: Independently search the case name to confirm it appears in a real court docket or known settlement website rather than clicking any link in the message
Visit the official settlement website directly by typing the URL yourself instead of following a link from an email or text

Never provide a Social Security number or bank account information to claim a settlement "” legitimate administrators only need basic contact info and rarely need such details until payment time, and even then only through secure channels
Remember that genuine settlements never require you to pay a fee or wire money to receive funds you're owed
If you suspect it's a scam, don't respond, and report it to the FTC via reportfraud.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: Scammers send unsolicited emails, texts, or social media messages designed to look like official class-action settlement notices, claiming the recipient is eligible for a cash payout from a lawsuit. The messages mimic real settlement administrator communications but push victims to click a link where they're asked to hand over sensitive information like Social Security numbers and bank account details, or to pay an upfront "processing" fee before their winnings can supposedly be sent. In reality, legitimate settlements never require payment to receive money owed, and genuine claim forms only need basic contact information for mailing a check or payment.
redFlags: Request for a Social Security number or full bank account details to "process" a settlement payment
Any demand for an upfront processing fee or wiring money before funds are released
Missing case details such as case number, court name, law firm names, or no official settlement website
A notice received by email, text, or social media about a case the recipient wasn't previously aware of
realExamples: ConsumerAffairs reported in October 2025 that scammers were sending emails and texts claiming recipients were eligible for class-action settlement payments, using the claims to harvest personal data or raid bank accounts
reports.source: ConsumerAffairs, https://www.consumeraffairs.com/news/beware-scammers-exploiting-class-action-settlement-notices-to-harvest-your-data-102925.html

reports.title: Fake Invoice & Subscription Renewal Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send consumers and businesses fake invoices or "subscription renewal" emails for purchases or memberships that were never made, pushing victims to call a bogus support number or enter payment details to "resolve" the charge.
safetyTips: Verify any renewal or invoice by going directly to the company's official website to find its phone number, rather than using links or numbers in the email
Keep careful track of your purchase history and active subscriptions through bank statements or another budgeting method so you can spot a fake notice
Don't be easily intimidated by language claiming legal action will be taken for nonpayment; take time to confirm an invoice before sending money
Businesses should create a procedure for inspecting incoming invoices and verifying products or services were actually ordered and delivered before paying
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive an email or invoice that looks like it's from a familiar company stating a subscription needs to be renewed, often with an urgent warning about "late fees" if they don't act, leading the recipient to click a link and enter payment information. Another version involves a receipt for a large purchase the recipient doesn't remember making, prompting them to call a company's help number, where a scammer asks for personal and payment information to "resolve the issue." A business variant involves sending a small-dollar invoice for something generic like "office supplies" that appears to come from a typical vendor, hoping an accounting department pays it without double-checking.
redFlags: Unexpected invoice or renewal notice for a purchase or subscription you don't remember making
Urgent language about late fees or needing to act to avoid being charged
Customer service phone number or payment link embedded directly in the email rather than sourced independently
Request to pay without the ability to confirm the invoice is legitimate
realExamples: A consumer receives an email stating a subscription needs to be renewed to avoid 'late fees,' appearing to come from a familiar company, leading the recipient to click a link and enter payment information.

BBB's Scam Tracker Risk Report found invoice scams were the second riskiest scam reported by businesses in 2025, costing businesses a median amount of $532, with PayPal the most frequently impersonated organization and 15.2% of reports involving fake invoice scams.
reports.source: BBB via KY3, https://www.ky3.com/2026/10/13/your-side-bbb-warns-fake-invoice-subscription-renewal-scams/

reports.title: Money Mule Recruitment Scam
reports.summary: Criminals recruit ordinary people — through fake remote jobs, online romances, or impersonation schemes — to receive and forward stolen money through their personal bank accounts, making the recruit a "money mule" who can face prosecution and financial liability.
relatedScams: Gold Bar & Bulk Cash Courier Scam
safetyTips: Never use your personal bank account to receive or transfer money for someone you have not met in person
Be extremely skeptical of remote job offers involving "payment processing" or "funds transfer" duties, especially if they require opening a new bank account
Don't send money to, or move money for, an online love interest or unverified acquaintance, even if they send you money first
If you think you've been used as a money mule, stop all communication and transactions immediately and notify your bank and law enforcement
Report suspected money mule activity to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3.gov), the FTC (reportfraud.ftc.gov), and the FDIC OIG Hotline
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters recruit "money mules" either knowingly or through deception to move the proceeds of fraud through the U.S. financial system. According to the FDIC OIG, criminals convince scam victims — often elderly, college students, or financially vulnerable people — to send money under false pretenses into mule accounts rather than directly to the criminals, which obscures the criminals' identities, and in some schemes criminals even dispatch couriers to physically retrieve cash, gold, or other valuables from victims while posing as law enforcement or bank officials. Separately, mules themselves are recruited intentionally or through deception, commonly by targeting job seekers with offers of convenient remote work such as a "rebates or payments processor," as well as targeting students, people on dating websites, the elderly, and individuals facing financial hardship. Once a mule receives funds or collects physical assets, they are instructed to withdraw cash, buy cryptocurrency, purchase gift cards, transfer funds through additional accounts, or send money overseas — layering transactions designed to conceal the illicit origin of the funds.
redFlags: Being asked to use a personal bank account to receive or move money for someone you have never met in person
Job postings involving "payment processing" or "funds transfer" work that require using or opening your own bank account
Unsolicited messages from strangers -- romantic partners, investment advisers, or purported government officials -- directing you to handle funds
Pressure to act quickly, secrecy about the reason for a transaction, or inconsistent explanations
Requests to convert funds to cryptocurrency, gift cards, wire transfers, or cash withdrawals
Being told to hand over cash, gold, or other valuables to a courier sent to your home, especially when the caller claims to be a government or bank employee
realExamples: FDIC OIG describes schemes where criminals dispatch couriers to physically retrieve cash, gold, or other valuables from victims, sometimes posing as law enforcement or bank officials, while directing the collected funds or assets through money mule accounts

FDIC OIG describes criminals recruiting money mules by offering convenient remote work opportunities, such as a "rebates or payments processor," often targeting students, job seekers, people on dating websites, the elderly, and individuals experiencing financial hardship
reports.source: FDIC Office of Inspector General, "Public Service Alert: Money Mules", https://www.fdicoig.gov/alerts/public-service-alert-money-mules

reports.title: Fake Business "Annual Report" Filing Notice Scam
reports.summary: Small business owners receive official-looking mailed notices demanding payment for "annual report" or "annual statement" filings from fake companies impersonating state agencies, often charging far more than the real government fee.
relatedScams: Fake Class Action Settlement Notice Scam
safetyTips: File annual reports and renewals only directly through your state's official Secretary of State or business-filing website, never through a link or QR code in unsolicited mail
Verify any company requesting a filing fee by checking your state's registered business entity database
Confirm the real, current fee for your state's annual report before paying anything
Report suspicious filing notices to your state Attorney General or Secretary of State's office
Sign up for official email or text alerts from your state's business filing portal so you can distinguish real notices from scams
reports.howItWorks: Scammers operating under generic-sounding names like "Business Filing LLC," "New Business Filing LLC," or "National Filing Corp" mail business owners and registered agents letters designed to look like official state notices (titled things like "Annual Statement Past Due" or "[State] Annual Report"). The letters claim a business filing fee is due, often using state seals, bureaucratic language, and urgent deadlines to appear legitimate, and direct the recipient to pay a steep fee — sometimes $125 to $175 or more — by mail or by scanning a QR code, even though the real state filing is free or costs only a small fraction of that amount when done directly through the Secretary of State's website. Some variants, such as the Michigan version, arrive in plain white envelopes with no return address. State agencies across the country, including Michigan, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Connecticut, Washington, South Carolina and Virginia, have issued repeated warnings as the scam resurfaces every few years under new company names.
redFlags: Notice arrives by mail in a plain envelope with no return address and demands payment via QR code
Company name sounds like a government office (e.g., 'Business Filing LLC') but is not actually a state agency
Fee requested is far higher than the state's actual annual report/filing fee
Letter creates urgency by threatening 'bad standing,' penalties, or loss of business status if not paid quickly
Official-sounding seals or letterhead that don't match the real agency's actual letterhead or domain
realExamples: Michigan businesses received fake 'Annual Statement Past Due' mailings in plain white envelopes with QR codes for payment, impersonating the state's LARA agency, as warned about in a Spring 2025 legal alert
North Carolina's Secretary of State warned in 2026 about misleading letters from 'Business Filing LLC' seeking $154 fees to file company annual reports

Pennsylvania's Department of State flagged mailings titled 'Pennsylvania Annual Report' from a company called 'New Business Filing LLC' that is not registered with the state, and a related site charging $136-plus for LLC filings
Connecticut officials have repeatedly warned about a recurring 'government imposter' business filing scam, first flagged in 2019 and renewed again in 2023 and 2024 under different fake entity names

Washington State's Attorney General and Secretary of State warned in December 2024 about letters targeting business registration, verification, and annual filings, some including QR codes linking to lookalike '.org' sites
reports.source: Pennsylvania Department of State, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dos/alerts-and-notices/business-and-charities-scams

reports.title: Booking.com WhatsApp Hotel Payment Scam
reports.summary: Scammers use real reservation details leaked in a Booking.com data breach to send convincing WhatsApp messages claiming a guest's hotel payment failed, directing them to a fake payment page that steals their card details.
safetyTips: Never enter card details through a WhatsApp link for an existing stay
Verify any WhatsApp sender's number against the hotel's official contact details
