Check that a payment link's web address matches the legitimate hotel or platform exactly before entering any information
Report suspicious messages to the Policía Nacional or Guardia Civil, or flag them through INCIBE's helpline
reports.howItWorks: After a Booking.com data breach, criminals send travelers a WhatsApp message that references their actual hotel name, exact stay dates, and real confirmation number, then claims there's a problem with the payment and includes a link to a fake site made to look like the hotel's or Booking.com's own payment page. Because the message gets so many real details correct, victims have little reason to doubt it and enter their card information to "fix" the supposed payment problem, handing it directly to the fraudsters. Investigators also traced some of the stolen details to hotel staff accounts compromised separately through phishing or malware, meaning the scam isn't limited to travelers who stayed during the breach window.
redFlags: Unsolicited WhatsApp message claiming your hotel card payment failed or needs to be redone
Message includes a link to re-enter payment details on a page designed to look like the hotel's or Booking.com's own payment page
The sender knows accurate booking details (hotel name, dates, confirmation number) but contacts you through WhatsApp rather than the official app
Request for payment or card verification outside Booking.com's official app or website
realExamples: An April 2026 Booking.com data breach exposed personal details of more than 4,000 travelers, including about 300 cases with payment card information, which scammers then used to craft convincing WhatsApp messages referencing travelers' real hotel name, stay dates, and confirmation number

Spain's INCIBE and Guardia Civil renewed a public warning on August 13, 2026 about the scam still actively targeting travelers that summer, with Spain's consumer group OCU logging complaints from travelers who lost hundreds of euros after trusting messages containing accurate stay details
reports.source: Home Exchange, https://www.homeexchange.com/blog/news-4000-travelers-exposed-the-whatsapp-hotel-scam-still-active-this-summer/

reports.title: VA Disability Claims "Pension Poaching" Fee Scam
reports.summary: Scammers posing as benefits "advisors," attorneys, or financial planners charge illegal fees or pressure veterans to sign over part of their VA disability or pension benefits in exchange for help filing a claim that is actually free through the VA.
safetyTips: Remember that applying for VA benefits is always free; VA does not charge claimants to complete the application process
Make sure all your benefits go directly to you (the veteran or beneficiary) and no one else, rather than to a caregiver's account
If you need assistance, contact VA directly through its national call center (1-800-827-1000) for help and advice completing a benefits application
Report suspicious activity to the VA Office of Inspector General (OIG) at va.gov/oig/hotline
If you believe you've been the victim of a dishonest financial planner or other dishonest actor, file a complaint with the Federal Trade Commission at www.consumercomplaints.ftc.gov
reports.howItWorks: A veteran is approached by someone posing as a caregiver, attorney, or financial planner who offers to help them qualify for or apply for VA benefits. Some scammers ask the veteran to pay an illegal fee for filing and submitting a VA benefits application, while others ask that future VA benefit payments be deposited directly into the scammer's or a caregiver's bank account instead of the veteran's own account. In reality, applying for VA benefits is always free, and VA does not charge claimants to complete the process; veterans can get help for free directly through VA's national call center. Falling for these scams can also lead to long-term consequences, since VA reviews the terms and conditions of assets transferred within three years before a pension claim is filed, which can disqualify a veteran from benefits they were once eligible to receive.
redFlags: Being asked to pay a fee just to apply for or help complete a VA benefits application
Requests to have your VA benefit payments deposited into a caregiver's or someone else's bank account instead of your own
Individuals posing as caregivers, attorneys, or financial planners offering to help you "qualify" for or apply for VA benefits for a fee
Encouragement to place your assets into investments that provide the "advisor" with lucrative fees
realExamples: VA News reporting that pension poaching perpetrators pose as caregivers, attorneys, or financial planners to get veterans to transfer benefit payments to them or pay an illegal application fee
reports.source: VA News, https://news.va.gov/111196/prevent-pension-poaching-fraud-protect-benefits/

reports.title: Fake U.S. Supreme Court Letter Scam
reports.summary: Scammers are mailing personally-addressed "certificates" on forged U.S. Supreme Court letterhead, complete with fake signatures of real justices, to pressure Social Security recipients into sending money or personal information.
relatedScams: Senior U.S. Official Impersonation Messaging Scam
safetyTips: Know that the Supreme Court does not contact individuals about criminal investigations, bank freezes, or Social Security numbers by letter, text, or email
Never send money, gift cards, or personal/financial details based on an unsolicited "legal" letter
Report the letter to the SSA Office of the Inspector General and keep it as evidence instead of discarding it
Talk to someone you trust before paying or responding to any letter that demands urgent action involving your money or identity
reports.howItWorks: The scam arrives as a physical letter styled as an official "certificate" on counterfeit U.S. Supreme Court letterhead bearing forged signatures of real sitting justices. It is personally addressed to the recipient and falsely claims they are a "primary suspect" in criminal legal proceedings tied to identity theft and that their Social Security number has been compromised, sometimes invoking a real-sounding but misnamed federal agency and a named state attorney general for added legitimacy. The letter may use the real name of an actual SSA executive to appear authentic and claims the Supreme Court has ordered banks to freeze the recipient's assets, telling them they cannot hold more than $10,000 in any bank account or $80,000–$100,000 in investments. It pressures the victim to urgently cooperate with a named "SSA official," ultimately to send money or hand over sensitive personal/financial information, falsely claiming SSA will issue them a new Social Security number. Scammers most likely follow up with text messages or telephone calls.
redFlags: Unsolicited letter claiming to be from the U.S. Supreme Court
Letter is labeled a "certificate" and uses forged justice signatures
Claims you are a criminal suspect and must act urgently to avoid losing your assets
Demands you keep account balances under specific dollar thresholds or cooperate with a named official
References a misnamed federal agency (e.g., the "Drug Enforcement Agency" instead of the correct name)
Pressure to send money or share personal/financial information quickly
realExamples: The SSA Office of the Inspector General issued an October 8, 2025 alert describing letters on fake Supreme Court letterhead with forged signatures of Chief Justice John Roberts and Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor, claiming recipients were primary suspects in legal proceedings overseen by a named state attorney general.

Reported versions of the letter claimed recipients could not hold more than $10,000 in any bank account or $80,000–$100,000 in investments, and asserted the Supreme Court had ordered financial institutions to freeze the recipient's assets, referencing an incorrectly named 'Drug Enforcement Agency' and the Department of the Treasury.
reports.source: Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General, https://oig.ssa.gov/scam-alerts/2025-10-08-unexpected-letter-text-or-email-from-the-u-s-supreme-court-think-scam-first/

reports.title: Midterm Election Campaign & Voter Registration Scam
reports.summary: Ahead of the 2026 U.S. midterms, the FBI warns scammers are impersonating candidates and campaigns using AI-cloned voices, fake political action committees, and phony voter-registration pages to steal donations, money, and personal data.
safetyTips: Verify any Political Action Committee, Party Committee, or Candidate Committee's registration and financial filings directly on the Federal Election Commission (FEC) website before donating
Remember that campaign donations are not investments \u2014 they will not increase in value or be returned
Never click links in unsolicited texts or emails about voter registration; go directly to your state's official election website to check or update your registration
Do not provide personally identifiable information to callers, texters, or emailers you don't know, even if they reference a candidate or election deadline
Be skeptical of merchandise offers tied to campaigns that require upfront payment with vague delivery promises
reports.howItWorks: The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) issued a PSA warning that scammers are impersonating political campaigns, using AI-generated voices, images, and messages to create convincing fake solicitations for donations, undelivered merchandise, or voter registration schemes designed to harvest personally identifiable information
redFlags: A text or email claims you are not registered to vote and links to an unfamiliar "voter registration" page asking for personal details
A "campaign" or PAC guarantees your donation will grow in value or be paid back as a financial return
Someone encourages you to recruit others to "invest" in a political fund to increase your payout share
Unsolicited calls or messages using a candidate's cloned voice, image, or slogan to pressure urgent donations
Pressure to act quickly, before you can verify the campaign or PAC through official channels
realExamples: The FBI's October 15, 2026 PSA (an update to a 2024 election-cycle alert) described schemes where victims are promised financial returns on "investments" in campaign pools, only to lose funds or have their data compromised
A described voter-data scheme uses a text or email claiming the recipient isn't registered to vote and links to a fake state voter registration page to steal PII for identity theft
The FBI noted scammers use candidate names, images, logos and slogans to solicit fake campaign contributions and sell merchandise that is never delivered
reports.source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) PSA, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA261015-3 ; Help Net Security, https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/10/16/usa-2026-midterm-election-scams/

reports.title: Fake "Is This Still Available" Marketplace Name-Lure Scam
reports.summary: Scammers text victims a fabricated Facebook Marketplace listing that uses the victim's own name as the "seller," hoping the urge to correct the mistake will trigger a reply that confirms the phone number is active.
safetyTips: Don't reply to unexpected texts about items you never listed, even to say 'wrong number' or 'that's not me' — any reply confirms your number is active
Open Facebook independently to inspect Marketplace activity, recent logins, messages, email addresses, phone numbers, and recovery settings rather than tapping links or images sent in a text
If you find a profile genuinely impersonating you, preserve the URL and report it to Facebook through its impersonation-reporting tools
Limit what you share publicly on social media, since scammers can use that information to increase the credibility of their attempts
Don't click a link, call a number supplied in the conversation, scan a QR code, or share a one-time code or screenshot of a security message
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive an unsolicited text (often via iMessage) asking "Is this still available for purchase?" with an attached screenshot of what looks like a real Facebook Marketplace listing. When the recipient looks closely, the "seller" name on the listing matches their own name, even though the profile photo belongs to a different person. Malwarebytes researchers describe this as a "conversation lure" — a message crafted to feel personal so the recipient reacts with "that isn't me" and replies to correct it. Researchers believe scammers pair names with phone numbers obtained from data breaches to mass-produce these personalized fake listings, and that AI tools now make it cheap and fast to generate convincing, individualized screenshots at scale for huge lists of targets. Once a victim replies at all — even just to say "wrong number" or "that's not me" — it confirms the number is active and being monitored, making it a more valuable target that can be resold to other scammers or used in other cybercrimes such as downloading malware, beginning a relationship that leads to fraud, or taking over the victim's Facebook account.
redFlags: Unsolicited text with a Marketplace or classifieds screenshot asking if an item is 'still available'
The listing shows your own name as the seller for an item you never posted
Profile photo attached to the listing doesn't match the name or doesn't look familiar
Message arrives from an unknown number with no prior context or relationship
Urge to reply immediately to 'correct' the mistaken impersonation
realExamples: Malwarebytes researcher Pieter Arntz documented a case where a recipient got an iMessage asking "Is this still available for purchase?" with a fabricated Marketplace listing showing their own name as the seller, paired with an unrelated person's profile photo of the same name.
reports.source: Malwarebytes Threat Intelligence, https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/10/facebook-marketplace-phish-uses-your-name-and-number

reports.title: Mortgage Closing Wire Fraud Scam
reports.summary: Scammers hack real estate professionals' email accounts to monitor upcoming home closings, then send homebuyers spoofed last-minute wiring instructions that divert their down payment and closing funds into fraudulent accounts.
relatedScams: SEO Poisoning Bank Account Takeover Scam
safetyTips: Identify two trusted individuals (your real estate and settlement agents) ahead of closing and agree on a phone number or code phrase to confirm any payment instructions, rather than trusting email alone
Call the title company or real estate agent using a phone number you previously agreed to \u2014 never a number or link from an email \u2014 before wiring any funds
Avoid clicking on any links or downloading attachments without first confirming with your trusted representatives, and do not email financial information since email is never a secure way to send it

If you've already wired funds and suspect fraud, immediately contact your bank or wire-transfer company to request a wire recall and file a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3.gov)
reports.howItWorks: According to the CFPB, scammers are increasingly targeting real estate professionals, seeking to compromise their email in order to monitor email correspondences with clients and identify upcoming real estate transactions. During the closing process, scammers send spoofed emails to homebuyers, posing as the real estate agent, settlement agent, legal representative, or another trusted individual, with false instructions for wiring closing funds, aiming to divert the homebuyer's closing costs and down payment into a fraudulent account.
redFlags: Receiving an email with last-minute changes to wiring instructions right before your closing date
A real estate agent, settlement agent, or legal representative asks you to send closing funds via a new or different account than previously discussed
Being asked to confirm closing instructions, including account name and number, by email instead of in person or by a previously agreed phone number
realExamples: CFPB describes scammers compromising real estate professionals' email accounts to monitor correspondence and identify upcoming transactions, then sending spoofed emails posing as the real estate agent, settlement agent, or legal representative to send false instructions for wiring closing funds
reports.source: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/blog/mortgage-closing-scams-how-protect-yourself-and-your-closing-funds/

reports.title: Negative Google Review Extortion Scam
reports.summary: Scammers flood a small business's Google Business Profile with fake one-star reviews, then contact the owner demanding payment, goods, or services to make the bad reviews disappear.
relatedScams: Impersonation Credit Repair Scheme (Fake Debt Collector/Creditor)
safetyTips: Never pay or engage with the scammers to have reviews removed -- payment rarely stops the attacks and can invite more
Take and keep screenshots of the fake reviews and any related messages (emails, texts, WhatsApp) to document the harassment or extortion attempt
Report suspicious reviews to Google using the "report review" option directly in Google Maps, providing details explaining why it's fake
Report extortion attempts using Google's official merchant extortion report form
Consider removing your cellphone number from online listings, as this has helped stop WhatsApp harassment for at least one victim
reports.howItWorks: The attack typically starts with "review-bombing," where fraudsters flood a business's Google listing with inauthentic one-star reviews, often using copy-and-paste language across multiple fake accounts whose profiles may lack photos, have few past reviews, or show reviews scattered across unrelated industries and locations. Once the business's rating has visibly dropped, the scammers reach out directly to the owner, frequently through third-party messaging apps like WhatsApp, and demand money to remove the negative reviews. They threaten that if the business doesn't pay, the fake reviews will stay up or the attack will escalate further, pressuring owners who fear reputational damage into paying even though victims report the cycle does not stop once they pay.
redFlags: A sudden, unexplained spike in one-star reviews appearing all at once
Multiple negative reviews containing repeated or nearly identical copy-and-paste wording
Reviewer profiles with no profile photo, few past reviews, or reviews scattered across unrelated industries and locations
Someone contacting the business owner via WhatsApp or another third-party messaging app demanding payment to remove reviews
Threats that more fake reviews will be posted or the attack will escalate if payment isn't made
realExamples: A Los Angeles contractor received a WhatsApp message from a number in Pakistan warning that someone had ordered 20 negative reviews of her business; her once-perfect 5-star Google rating soon plunged to 3.6, and she paid $250 in two separate payments before realizing the cycle would not stop.

A moving company owner in Georgia received a WhatsApp message from a man who later admitted to selling negative Google reviews for $100 per batch of 20; the fake reviews described elaborate false complaints like boxes smashed in front of customers, and new fakes kept appearing even after Google removed some.
reports.source: Google Fraud and Scams Advisory, November 2025, https://blog.google/technology/safety-security/fraud-and-scams-advisory-november-2025/ ; ConsumerAffairs, https://www.consumeraffairs.com/news/small-businesses-hit-by-global-scam-of-fake-negative-google-reviews-091125.html

reports.title: "Phantom Hacker" Three-Stage Tech/Bank/Government Imposter Scam
reports.summary: A multi-layered scam where fraudsters pose first as tech support, then a bank or brokerage, then a U.S. government agency to convince victims their money is at risk and must be moved to a "safe" account that scammers actually control.
relatedScams: Financial Institution Support Impersonation Account Takeover Scam
safetyTips: Do not click on unsolicited pop-ups, links in texts, or email attachments claiming your device or accounts are compromised
Never call a phone number provided in a pop-up, text, or unsolicited email — look up the real number yourself
Never allow a stranger who contacted you to install software or take remote control of your computer
Independently verify any claim that your financial accounts are compromised by calling your bank or brokerage directly using a number from your card or statement
Remember that no legitimate government agency will ever ask you to wire money, buy cryptocurrency, or send cash/gift cards to 'protect' your funds
If you've already sent money, report it immediately to your financial institution and file a complaint with the FBI's IC3.gov
reports.howItWorks: The FBI describes the "Phantom Hacker" scam as unfolding in three coordinated steps. A scammer posing as a customer support representative from a legitimate technology company initiates contact with the victim through a phone call, text, email, or a pop-up window on their computer and instructs the victim to call a number for "assistance."
redFlags: Unsolicited pop-up, text, or email claiming your computer or accounts have been hacked
Being told to download remote-access software so 'tech support' can fix a problem
A second caller claiming to be from your bank or brokerage saying your account was hacked by a foreign actor
Instructions to move money into a 'safe' third-party account, often described as held by the Federal Reserve or another government agency
Pressure to use wire transfer, cash, or conversion to cryptocurrency, sometimes sent overseas
Being told not to tell anyone (including bank staff) the real reason you're moving money
A third scammer posing as a government official sending fake official-looking letters or emails to keep the scheme going
realExamples: The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center reported that between January and June 2023 it received 19,000 tech support scam complaints with losses over $542 million, with victims over 60 comprising about half of victims and 66% of losses.

In 2025, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center received over 47,000 reports related to tech support scams, resulting in nationwide losses exceeding $2.1 billion, with about half of the victims and losses involving individuals aged 60 and older.
GuideStone Financial Resources said it had recently detected and stopped a Phantom Hacker fraud attempt targeting one of its members before any funds were moved.
reports.source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) PSA, https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2023/PSA230929; Yahoo News/FBI 2025 Internet Crime Report coverage, https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/fbi-says-phantom-hacker-scam-112500417.html

reports.title: Gift Card Draining Scam
reports.summary: Scammers secretly record or expose the codes on gift cards still sitting on store racks, then drain the funds the moment an unsuspecting shopper buys and activates the card. The FTC reports that gift cards were mentioned in at least one-quarter of recent fraud complaints, and the D.C. Attorney General's office has issued a warning about this "draining" scheme this holiday season.
relatedScams: Brushing Scam with QR Code Twist
safetyTips: Before buying, run your finger over the card's back and barcode to check for signs of tampering or a sticker applied on top
Buy gift cards at checkout counters, from cards locked away at stores, or directly from the retailer's official website instead of from open floor racks
Save your receipt and original packaging, which are critical if you need to report fraud to the retailer or the FTC
Register the gift card online if the retailer offers that option, and don't delay using the balance
Never purchase or send gift cards to pay a bill, fine, debt, or any government agency — no legitimate business or government agency will ever demand payment via gift card
Check gift card balances only through official websites or phone numbers printed on the card, not through links sent by text, email, or social media
reports.howItWorks: Before a gift card is ever purchased, a scammer takes it off an in-store display rack and either scratches off the back panel to expose the redemption code (then carefully resealing it) or uses a handheld scanner to capture the card number and PIN through the packaging; some scammers also place a fake barcode sticker over the real one so that any value loaded at checkout actually routes to a card the criminal controls. The card is then returned to the rack looking untouched. The scammer periodically checks the balance, including by calling the retailer's 800 number, to see when the card has been activated. Once activated, the scammer accesses the card online and steals the money, or clones the card, or diverts the funds to their own account, leaving the buyer or gift recipient with an empty or worthless card. Separately, no legitimate business or government agency will ever demand payment via gift card, and scammers may impersonate law enforcement, the IRS, tech support, or a family member to pressure victims into paying this way.
redFlags: A gift card's packaging looks damaged, opened, resealed, or shows a scratched-off or exposed PIN
You can feel or see a sticker layered on top of the card's real barcode
The card shows no funds or a drained balance after purchase and activation
Anyone (claiming to be law enforcement, the IRS, tech support, or a relative) demands payment specifically via gift card
A website offering to check your gift card's balance asks for the card's ID number and PIN or security code
realExamples: The D.C. Attorney General's office issued a December 2025 news release warning that scammers take an unpurchased gift card off the rack, scratch off the code, and cover it back up before it's bought and drained online.

The BBB shared a report on its Scam Tracker describing a gift card whose packaging looked untouched but had a sticker hidden under the barcode window that redirected funds away from the real card, leaving the card with no funds on it.
reports.source: FTC-cited consumer warning via myncu.com, https://www.myncu.com/explore/blog/gift-card-scams-are-rising-ftc-issues-new-fraud-warning ; WTOP News, https://wtop.com/consumer-news/2025/12/a-warning-about-a-new-gift-card-scam-called-draining-2/ ; BBB, https://www.bbb.org/all/consumer/tip/what-to-know-before-purchasing-a-gift-card

reports.title: Fake BianLian Ransomware Extortion Letter Scam
reports.summary: Criminals mail physical "ransom letters" to corporate executives falsely claiming to be the BianLian ransomware gang, saying they stole sensitive company data and demanding a Bitcoin payment via QR code within 10 days or the data will be leaked.
safetyTips: Do not scan the QR code or send any payment based solely on a mailed letter; verify independently with your IT/security team whether any breach actually occurred
Notify corporate executives and staff across the organization that this mail scam exists so no one pays out of panic
Report the letter to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and preserve the envelope and letter as evidence
If you have real concerns about a breach, check for actual indicators of compromise through your cybersecurity team rather than relying on the letter's claims
Treat any extortion demand delivered through an unusual or old-fashioned channel (postal mail) with extra suspicion since legitimate ransomware groups almost never contact victims this way
reports.howItWorks: Scammers send a letter through the U.S. Postal Service directly to a company's CEO or other executives, stamped "Time Sensitive Read Immediately." The letter claims the "BianLian Group" — a real, well-known Russia-linked ransomware gang — breached the organization's network and stole thousands of sensitive files. It threatens to publish the stolen data on BianLian's dark-web leak site unless a ransom of between $250,000 and $500,000 is paid within ten days, using an enclosed QR code that links to a Bitcoin wallet, and states the group "will not negotiate further" with the recipient. In reality, the FBI and USPIS found no connection between the letter senders and the actual BianLian group; the return address traces to a mailbox in Boston, Massachusetts, and investigators noted the writing style doesn't match real BianLian ransom notes. The scam relies on executives panicking over a supposed data breach and paying before verifying whether any real intrusion occurred.
redFlags: An unsolicited physical letter stamped "Time Sensitive Read Immediately" claiming a cyberattack already occurred
A QR code directing payment to a Bitcoin wallet with a strict 10-day deadline
Claims that the group "will not negotiate" and demands an exact sum between $250,000 and $500,000
No corroborating evidence of an actual network breach, unusual system activity, or data exfiltration alerts
Return address tied to a generic suite/mailbox address rather than any verifiable organization
realExamples: The FBI issued a PSA (Alert I-030625b-PSA) describing letters mailed to corporate executives, primarily in the healthcare sector, claiming to be from the BianLian Group and demanding payment via an enclosed Bitcoin QR code within 10 days

The U.S. Postal Inspection Service confirmed letters were mailed with a Boston, Massachusetts return address under the name "BianLian Group" and stated no link was found between the senders and the real ransomware gang
Security researchers including Guidepoint Security and Arctic Wolf reported receiving scans of identical letters sent to CEOs, with envelopes postmarked in late February 2025
reports.source: FBI/CISA Alert, https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/06/fbi-warns-data-extortion-scam-targeting-corporate-executives

reports.title: BADBOX 2.0 Infected IoT Device Botnet Scam
reports.summary: Cheap, off-brand smart TV boxes, projectors, car infotainment units, and digital picture frames sold online come pre-loaded with hidden malware that secretly turns your home network into a criminal proxy used for fraud and other crimes.
safetyTips: Avoid downloading or sideloading apps from unofficial marketplaces that advertise free streaming content
Keep device operating systems, firmware, and apps updated, and never disable built-in malware protections like Google Play Protect

Periodically monitor your home network's internet traffic for suspicious or unexplained activity and assess all IoT devices connected to home networks for suspicious activity, disconnecting any device you suspect is compromised
Report suspected compromised devices or related criminal activity to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov
reports.howItWorks: Criminals compromise low-cost, often Chinese-manufactured Internet of Things (IoT) devices such as TV streaming boxes, digital projectors, aftermarket vehicle infotainment systems, and digital picture frames, either by pre-loading malicious software onto the device before a consumer ever buys it, or by hiding a backdoor inside an app the device downloads during setup. Once the device connects to a victim's home Wi-Fi, it can be pulled into the "BADBOX 2.0" botnet, and criminals then sell or give away access to that compromised home network's internet connection, routing other criminals' malicious traffic through the unsuspecting victim's residential IP address to disguise it as legitimate activity and use it for other criminal purposes.
redFlags: The device was purchased from an unofficial or suspicious app marketplace rather than a certified app store
Setup instructions tell you to disable Google Play Protect or other built-in security settings
A generic, unbranded TV streaming device is advertised as 'unlocked' or able to access free premium content
The IoT device is from an unrecognizable or off-brand manufacturer
The Android device is not Google Play Protect certified
You notice unexplained or unusual internet traffic coming from a smart device on your home network
realExamples: The FBI's PSA warned that cyber criminals gained unauthorized access to home networks through compromised TV streaming devices, digital projectors, aftermarket vehicle infotainment systems, digital picture frames, and other products, most of which were manufactured in China.
reports.source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), "Home Internet Connected Devices Facilitate Criminal Activity," https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250605

reports.title: Google Business Profile Hijacking & Verification Scam
reports.summary: Scammers target small business owners by hijacking their Google Business Profile listings through fake ownership claims, phony "verification" calls, and suspension threats designed to steal control of the listing or extract payment.
safetyTips: Regularly audit who has owner or manager-level access to your Google Business Profile and remove anyone who no longer needs it
Reject any ownership or manager request you don't recognize immediately and investigate how it was sent, rather than approving it without scrutiny
Remember Google Business Profiles are always free to create and manage; never pay a fee to verify, restore, or maintain a listing
Google does not cold-call business owners about their listing, so treat any such call as suspicious and manage your listing by logging in directly at business.google.com
Enable two-factor authentication on the Google account tied to your business listing
reports.howItWorks: Scammers exploit the fact that Google allows anyone to request ownership or manager access to a business listing by clicking "Claim this business." If a scammer sends that request and an employee approves it without checking who sent it, the attacker gains full control and can change the listed phone number to reroute customer calls to themselves, alter the business address to send customers to a fake location, and lock the real owner out entirely. A second version of the scam arrives as a phone call or email claiming to be from Google business support, saying the listing has a problem, is at risk of being removed, is missing verification, or has seen suspicious activity — the caller or sender then asks for login credentials or a payment to "restore" or "fix" the account, even though Google Business Profiles are free to create and maintain and Google never cold-calls business owners or demands payment for profile maintenance.
redFlags: An unsolicited ownership or manager-access request appears in your Google Business Profile dashboard from an account you don't recognize
A caller or emailer claiming to be from Google says your listing has a problem, is at risk of removal, or is missing verification, and asks for your login credentials or payment to fix it
Any request for payment to "verify," "restore," or maintain your free Google Business listing
Pressure to act immediately without time to verify the request
A communication claiming to be from Google that arrives by phone call or from an email domain that isn't @google.com
realExamples: Scammers submit a fraudulent ownership claim to a Google Business Profile; once an employee approves the request without checking who sent it, the attacker changes the listed phone number to route calls to themselves, alters the business address to redirect customers, and locks the original owner out entirely
A caller claims to be from Google business support, saying the profile is at risk of being removed or is missing verification, and asks for login credentials or a payment to restore the account
reports.source: guard.io, "Google Business Profile Scams: What to Know," https://guard.io/blog/google-business-profile-review-listing-scams

reports.title: Fake Inheritance / Unclaimed Estate Phishing Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send polished, error-free emails claiming the recipient is a beneficiary of a large unclaimed inheritance or estate, sometimes impersonating state government employees, in order to extract upfront "release" fees or harvest personal data through phishing links.
safetyTips: Never click links or buttons in unexpected inheritance or estate emails; go directly to your state's official unclaimed property website instead
Do not pay any fee, tax, or charge to receive an inheritance "you didn't know you had" ", legitimate estates never require upfront payment to release funds
Verify any claimed government agency or employee by calling the agency directly using a number from its official .gov website, not one provided in the email
Be skeptical of deadlines pressuring you to act within hours; real legal and probate processes do not operate on urgent email countdowns
Report suspicious inheritance emails to the FTC, your state Attorney General, and forward phishing emails to the appropriate reporting address
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive an unsolicited, professional-looking email informing them they are a "Primary Potential Beneficiary" of an unclaimed inheritance or estate, often from a distant relative or tied to a fabricated organization. The message creates urgency with a short deadline, warning the funds will be forfeited or reassigned if the recipient doesn't act immediately, and includes a button or link to "claim" the money, which actually harvests personal and financial data. In a related, more elaborate version, scammers impersonate real state government employees (such as from an insurance department or banking agency) and a foreign credit union, telling an older victim a wealthy distant relative left them an inheritance, then pressuring them to wire upfront "release" fees through legitimate, licensed financial institutions over an extended period before any inheritance is ever paid out.
redFlags: Unsolicited email claiming you're owed a large unclaimed inheritance you never knew about
Artificial urgency, such as a short countdown (e.g., 48 hours) before funds are supposedly forfeited
Requests to click a button or link to 'check' or 'claim' your inheritance
Demands for upfront fees, taxes, or 'release' payments before any inheritance is delivered
Use of official-sounding but non-existent registry or agency names
Sender impersonating a government employee, bank, or foreign credit union representative
realExamples: A Fox News reader identified only as "Tim C." received a "Heir Research Registry" email claiming he was a "Primary Potential Beneficiary" of an unclaimed estate, with a 48-hour deadline and a "Check My Unclaimed Inheritance" button designed to steal his data.

Pennsylvania's Insurance Department, Department of Aging, Department of Banking and Securities, State Police, and Attorney General's Office jointly warned residents after an older Pennsylvanian received an email impersonating a Commonwealth employee and a foreign credit union representative, claiming a wealthy distant relative had left a large inheritance, then was pressured to pay upfront fees through licensed financial institutions totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars over nearly a year.
reports.source: Fox News (CyberGuy Report) https://www.foxnews.com/tech/inheritance-scam-email-looks-real-steals-data ; Pennsylvania Insurance Department https://www.pa.gov/agencies/insurance/newsroom/shapiro-administration-warns-pennsylvanians-scammers-fake-inheritance

reports.title: Fake Municipal Court "Unpaid Parking Ticket" Text Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send texts and emails pretending to be a municipal court, claiming you have an unpaid parking ticket and must pay immediately or face fines, license suspension, or a court appearance.
safetyTips: Do not click links in unsolicited texts or emails about court fines or parking tickets
Remember that government agencies generally do not conduct official business through unsolicited text messages and rarely use email unless you've requested it
If unsure whether a message is legitimate, contact the court or agency directly using a verified phone number, not one provided in the message
Report suspicious messages as spam/junk through your phone or email provider and block the sender
File a complaint with your state Attorney General's consumer protection office, including a copy of the message
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive a text message or email claiming to be from a municipal court — often impersonating the Philadelphia Municipal Court, though other courts or government agencies may be named — alleging they have an unpaid parking ticket requiring immediate payment or a court appearance. The message threatens escalating consequences for non-payment, such as additional fines, driver's license suspension, or court enforcement action, and includes a link for the recipient to "pay" the fine. The urgency and threat of legal trouble are designed to pressure the recipient into clicking the link and entering payment or personal information before they stop to verify whether the message is real.
redFlags: Unsolicited text message or email claiming to be from a municipal court about a parking ticket
Threats of license suspension, added fines, or a court appearance if you don't pay immediately
A link embedded in the message directing you to make a payment
Pressure to act fast using fear, urgency, and embarrassment
Government business being conducted via unexpected text or email rather than official mail
realExamples: Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday issued a public alert describing fraudulent texts and emails impersonating Philadelphia Municipal Court over alleged unpaid parking tickets

The fraudulent messages frequently included a link directing recipients to make a payment, and warned of consequences like additional fines, license suspension, or court enforcement action for non-payment
reports.source: Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General, "Attorney General Sunday Warns Pennsylvanians of Scam Messages Impersonating Municipal Court" - https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/taking-action/attorney-general-sunday-warns-pennsylvanians-of-scam-messages-impersonating-municipal-court/

reports.title: AI Obituary Mining "Graveyard Grift" Scam
reports.summary: Scammers use AI to scan published obituaries for details on recently widowed or bereaved people, then use that personal information to craft convincing fraud pitches targeting the grieving family. One widow lost over $7,000 after fraudsters claimed to have helped her late husband hide tax evasion.
relatedScams: Fake Inheritance / Unclaimed Estate Phishing Scam
safetyTips: Limit sensitive details in obituaries such as full names of relatives, specific employers, schools, and exact hometown to reduce what scammers can exploit
Establish a family rule that no unexpected payment request tied to a deceased relative's affairs is made until verified with another family member or trusted advisor

If someone calls asking for personal information and insists it be handled immediately, hang up; initiate any callback yourself using a number you look up independently rather than one given by the caller
Be extra cautious with financial decisions in the weeks after a loved one's death, when grief and administrative overload make it easier to be manipulated

If you believe you've been scammed, immediately contact your bank, brokerage, credit card company, or wire transfer company, and file complaints with law enforcement and consumer complaint organizations
reports.howItWorks: Fraudsters use artificial intelligence to rapidly scour online obituaries and death notices, extracting names of spouses, children, employers, hometowns, and other personal details that families publish to honor loved ones. The AI helps scammers quickly identify targets, write a personalized "scam script," and even generate deepfake images, voice messages, or videos, letting them send convincing phishing calls, texts, or emails to thousands of potential victims within minutes. Posing as officials or associates of the deceased, scammers then contact the surviving spouse claiming the departed left behind a hidden debt, tax problem, or legal issue that must be resolved immediately to protect the inheritance, pressuring the grieving person into an urgent payment before they have time to verify the claim with family or authorities.
redFlags: Unsolicited call or message shortly after a death claiming the deceased owed taxes or had a hidden financial/legal problem
Caller references specific personal details (relatives' names, employer, hometown) that match an obituary
Demand for urgent payment to 'protect' an inheritance or prevent legal consequences
Pressure to act alone without checking with another family member or financial advisor first
Request for wire transfer, gift cards, or other hard-to-trace payment tied to the deceased's supposed debt
realExamples: A widow lost more than $7,000 after scammers used her husband's obituary to identify her, then claimed they had helped him conceal tax evasion and that she needed to pay to preserve her inheritance, according to Truecaller spokesperson Clayton LiaBraaten speaking to USA Today.
reports.source: Moneywise, https://moneywise.com/news/top-stories/ai-scammers-obituaries-elderly-fraud-widows

reports.title: AI-Generated Fake Review Scam
reports.summary: Scammers and shady sellers use AI tools to mass-produce fake five-star product and service reviews that lure shoppers into buying low-quality goods or visiting fraudulent sites that steal payment and personal information.
safetyTips: Click on a reviewer's name or profile to check their posting history; real users typically leave a mix of ratings across varied products
Be suspicious of listings with only glowing five-star reviews and no critical or mixed feedback
Watch for unnatural timing patterns, like dozens of five-star reviews appearing all at once
Research the seller or website independently before entering payment or personal information, especially if the purchase was driven mainly by reviews
Treat reviews as only one data point and verify a company through official channels before buying
reports.howItWorks: Fraudulent sellers and website operators use generative AI to write large batches of realistic-sounding customer reviews for products or services that were never actually purchased or used. These reviews are posted on shopping sites, marketplaces, and review platforms to build false credibility and push shoppers toward a purchase. In some cases the fake-review scheme is just the bait for a larger scam: the glowing reviews drive traffic to a fraudulent website that, once a buyer tries to check out or "verify" their order, harvests credit card numbers and other personal details, leading to identity theft and financial fraud rather than just a disappointing product.
redFlags: Overly generic, gushing language with no specific details about how the product was used
Identical or nearly identical phrases repeated across multiple reviews for the same item
A sudden flood of five-star reviews posted within hours or days of each other
Reviewer profiles with only one or two reviews, often all five-star and for similar types of products
Reviews that sound 'too perfect' with no mention of downsides or imperfections
realExamples: State consumer protection officials report that businesses are increasingly using AI to generate customer reviews that are not based on real purchases, sometimes as part of larger schemes where fraudulent websites use the fake reviews to lure shoppers into purchases or sign-ups that end in theft of personal or financial information.
reports.source: Ohio Attorney General, Consumer Advocate Newsletter (December 2025), https://www.ohioattorneygeneral.gov/Media/Newsletters/Consumer-Advocate/December-2025/Beware-of-AI-generated-customer-reviews

reports.title: Fake Amazon Product Recall Text Scam
reports.summary: Scammers send text messages claiming a recent Amazon purchase has been "recalled" for safety reasons and urge recipients to click a link to get a refund, which actually leads to a fake Amazon login page designed to steal credentials and payment details.
safetyTips: Never click links in unsolicited recall or refund texts; instead open the official Amazon app or manually type amazon.com into your browser to check your orders and recall notices
Remember that legitimate recalls show up inside your Amazon account and never through random text links
Log in and check your recent orders, looking for recall notifications directly within your account, rather than trusting a link from a text message
Contact Amazon customer service through the official site if you're unsure about a recall text
Report suspicious texts to Amazon so they can investigate and shut down phishing networks
reports.howItWorks: Victims receive an unsolicited text (smishing) that references a recent order and claims the item has been recalled for safety reasons, urging the recipient to click a link to "start your refund" or "view recall details." That link leads to a very real-looking but completely fake Amazon login page. Once the victim enters their email and password, scammers can hijack the account, change the password, and potentially access stored payment methods. The pages often look nearly identical to Amazon's real website, which is why this scam catches people off guard.
redFlags: Recall notice arrives by text rather than through your Amazon account or official app
Message uses urgency and fear, such as claiming a product you bought was recalled for safety reasons, to get you to click fast
Link in the text leads to a login page instead of taking you through the official amazon.com site or app
Message promises a refund if you click through and enter your login information
realExamples: Guardio researchers, cited by ConsumerAffairs, found scammers sending texts claiming a recent purchase was included in an "official recall," which included a link to "start your refund" or "view recall details" that led to a fake Amazon sign-in page
reports.source: ConsumerAffairs, https://www.consumeraffairs.com/news/that-amazon-recall-alert-text-its-probably-a-scam-021826.html

reports.title: EBT/SNAP Card Skimming Scam
reports.summary: Criminals attach hidden skimming overlays to point-of-sale card readers at grocery stores and gas pumps to steal EBT/SNAP benefit card data and PINs, then clone the cards and drain victims' food assistance benefits before they can buy groceries.
relatedScams: Mail Theft Check Washing/Check Cooking Scam
safetyTips: Inspect ATMs, gas pumps, and point-of-sale terminals for anything loose, crooked, or damaged before inserting or swiping a card, and don't use one that looks unusual
Use tap-to-pay or chip-insert technology whenever possible instead of swiping, since skimmers mainly target the magnetic stripe

If using a debit card at a gas station, run it as a credit card to avoid entering a PIN; if that is not an option, use your hand to hide your PIN to block scammers who may be using tiny pinhole cameras above the keypad
Use ATMs in a well-lit, indoor location, which are less vulnerable targets
Be alert for skimming devices in tourist areas, which are popular targets
reports.howItWorks: Because many EBT cards still rely on outdated magnetic-stripe technology instead of chip or tap-to-pay, criminals place a thin, realistic-looking overlay device directly on top of a legitimate payment terminal's card slot and keypad, often disguised as part of the keypad on point-of-sale machines, making tampered machines difficult to detect. When a shopper swipes their EBT card and enters their PIN, the skimmer silently records the magnetic-stripe data, which scammers then encode onto another card with a magnetic strip. The cloned card is then used to drain the victim's benefits.
redFlags: A card reader's keypad or card slot looks loose, crooked, bulky, damaged, or scratched compared to the rest of the terminal
The terminal requires a magnetic-stripe swipe rather than offering chip insert or tap-to-pay as an option
Skimming devices are often embedded in point-of-sale machines and disguised as keypads, making tampered terminals hard to detect
Tourist areas and locations with high concentrations of small stores are popular targets for installed skimmers
realExamples: A U.S. Secret Service New York Field Office operation, along with law enforcement partners including the NYPD, NYC Department of Investigation, and USDA Office of Inspector General, concluded a three-day EBT fraud and payment card skimming outreach effort, removing 35 illegal devices (15 in Brooklyn, 9 in the Bronx, 10 in Queens, and one additional device in Manhattan) and preventing an estimated $36.5 million in potential losses; nationwide in 2025, law enforcement removed more than 400 illegal skimming devices, preventing an estimated $428 million in potential fraud losses
reports.source: U.S. Secret Service, https://www.secretservice.gov/newsroom/releases/2026/06/us-secret-service-new-york-field-office-skimming-operation-nets-35

reports.title: Ghost Tax Preparer Scam
reports.summary: Unscrupulous paid tax preparers inflate refunds with fake credits and deductions, then refuse to sign the return or include their PTIN — leaving the taxpayer legally holding the bag when the IRS comes calling.
relatedScams: Impersonation Credit Repair Scheme (Fake Debt Collector/Creditor)
safetyTips: Verify any paid preparer signs the return and enters a valid PTIN before you submit it
Never sign a blank or incomplete tax form
Be wary of preparers who exaggerate eligibility for deductions or promise credits you may not qualify for
Report suspected ghost preparers and preparer misconduct, or file a complaint about a tax return preparer, with the IRS
Rely on trusted sources and qualified tax professionals, not bad tax advice on social media
reports.howItWorks: A "ghost" preparer is paid to prepare a federal tax return but will not sign it or include a valid Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN), even though federal law requires any paid preparer to do both. When a preparer refuses to sign or provide a PTIN, that is a major red flag. These preparers often exploit credits by promising large refunds, and may exaggerate eligibility for deductions or claim credits that taxpayers do not qualify for, then disappear after filing, leaving the taxpayer responsible for penalties, interest, or audits. Because the taxpayer's name and Social Security number are on the return, the taxpayer — not the invisible preparer — is legally responsible for what is filed, and taxpayers should never sign a blank or incomplete return.
redFlags: Preparer refuses to sign the return or won't provide/include a valid PTIN
Asks you to sign a blank or incomplete return
Promises unusually large refunds by exaggerating eligibility for deductions or claiming credits the taxpayer doesn't qualify for
Disappears after filing, leaving the taxpayer responsible for penalties, interest, or audits
realExamples: The IRS's 2026 Dirty Dozen list includes ghost preparers as item #8, warning that when a preparer refuses to sign or provide a PTIN, that is a major red flag and the taxpayer is legally responsible for what is filed.
reports.source: IRS, "Be informed, not fooled by ghost preparers and tax credit scams" and "Dirty Dozen tax scams for 2026" https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/be-informed-not-fooled-by-ghost-preparers-and-tax-credit-scams ; https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/dirty-dozen-tax-scams-for-2026-irs-reminds-taxpayers-to-watch-out-for-dangerous-threats

reports.title: Digital Arrest Scam
reports.summary: Scammers impersonate police, CBI, customs, or court officials on a video call, falsely accuse the victim of a serious crime, and claim they are now under "digital arrest" — forcing them to stay on camera for hours or days while transferring their savings to "safe" accounts to prove innocence.
safetyTips: Know that no legitimate police force, court, or government investigator conducts arrests, hearings, or investigations over phone or video calls
Hang up immediately and independently verify by calling the agency directly using an official number, never one given by the caller
Never transfer money, share OTPs, or grant remote device access to anyone claiming to be law enforcement over a call
If pressured or isolated during a call, contact a trusted family member or the real local police in person before taking any action
Report suspicious calls to local cybercrime authorities or consumer protection agencies right away
reports.howItWorks: The scam begins with a phone call, often with a spoofed caller ID, in which the fraudster poses as a law-enforcement or government official and accuses the victim of a crime such as money laundering, drug trafficking, or sending illegal packages. The caller then escalates to a video call, displaying fake FIRs, arrest warrants, and official-looking IDs, and tells the victim they are now under "digital arrest" and must remain visible on camera and isolated from family or friends while their case is "investigated". Under sustained psychological pressure and threats of real arrest or criminal charges, victims are coerced into transferring money — sometimes repeatedly over days or weeks — into multiple "safe" bank accounts or converting funds to cryptocurrency, supposedly to verify their innocence or avoid prosecution, or into handing over OTPs, banking credentials, or remote access to their devices.
redFlags: A caller claims you can be "arrested" or investigated entirely through a phone or video call
You're told to stay on camera continuously and cut off contact with family or friends while the "investigation" proceeds
You're pressured to move money into "safe" government or police accounts, or to convert it to cryptocurrency
Fake documents like arrest warrants, FIRs, or official ID cards are shown on-screen to look legitimate
The caller uses urgency and threats of immediate arrest, asset freezing, or criminal charges to prevent you from hanging up or consulting anyone
realExamples: A 41-year-old Kolkata businessman lost INR 7.55 million over a 12-day digital arrest after scammers accused him of money laundering starting February 23, 2025, calling constantly and keeping him under surveillance until he made multiple transactions.
A reported ₹58.13 crore fraud investigated by Mumbai cyber-police targeted a 72-year-old victim, involving multiple arrests and the discovery of thousands of fake bank accounts used for laundering.
reports.source: ISACA Industry News, https://www.isaca.org/resources/news-and-trends/industry-news/2025/trapped-virtually-understanding-digital-arrest-scams; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_arrest_scam; Free Press Journal, https://www.freepressjournal.in/tech/digital-arrest-fraud-over-21900-complaints-involving-647-crore-registered-in-2026-centre-tells-supreme-court

reports.title: Fake Retail Coupon / Promo Code Scam
reports.summary: Scammers post counterfeit coupons and promo codes for well-known retail brands on social media, email, and fake websites to steal personal information, payment details, or spread malware instead of delivering real discounts.
relatedScams: Brushing Scam with QR Code Twist
safetyTips: Be skeptical of coupons offering steep discounts near or above an item's retail value
Verify any coupon directly on the retailer's official website or by calling their customer service line before using it
Never give personal or financial information to claim a coupon, and don't pay a membership fee for access to discount codes
Hover over (don't click) links in coupon emails or texts to check where they actually lead before visiting
reports.howItWorks: Scammers create ads or posts — often using a brand's real logo — that advertise an unusually steep discount, such as 80% off, at a popular retail store. After clicking the coupon or promo code link, the consumer either makes a purchase on a fake storefront that never ships the item, or is sent to a third-party site that asks them to enter personal and payment information in exchange for the coupon. In many cases the victim never receives any coupon or product; in others, a fake tracking number falsely shows the package as delivered, and the company becomes unreachable or stops responding when the buyer seeks a refund. Some versions require signing up for a paid coupon service with a monthly membership fee that promises digital or paper coupons that never arrive or turn out to be fake, while other variations involve sharing a link on social media in exchange for a coupon that leads to a third-party site collecting personal information.
redFlags: Discount is unusually large, near or above the item's actual retail value, like 80% off
Coupon or deal is only found through a social media ad or shared link rather than the brand's own website
You're asked to pay a monthly membership fee or provide personal/financial information in exchange for a coupon
realExamples: A BBB Scam Tracker report describes a consumer who placed an order via a TikTok promo code and never received their item; a tracking number showed the package as delivered on a Sunday, but nothing arrived, and the company stopped responding to emails
Another consumer reported ordering clothing through a Facebook discount ad and paying by credit card, but the order never arrived and the tracking information turned out not to be real
reports.source: Better Business Bureau, https://www.bbb.org/article/scams/22318-bbb-scam-alert-fake-retail-coupons-hit-social-media

reports.title: "Dark Sourcery" AI Chatbot Answer Poisoning Scam
reports.summary: Scammers are flooding the web with fake posts, PDFs, reviews, and support pages specifically engineered to get AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Google AI Overview to repeat fraudulent customer support phone numbers and login pages as if they were official company contact details.
relatedScams: SEO Poisoning Bank Account Takeover Scam
safetyTips: Never call a support number or click a login link that an AI chatbot or AI search summary gives you — go directly to the company's official app or website and find contact details there instead
Independently verify any phone number, email address, or URL for customer support, refunds, account recovery, or software downloads against the company's verified official channels before using it
Be especially cautious with AI-provided contact details for sensitive tasks like account recovery, payments, refunds, or software updates, since these are the exact categories attackers are targeting
If you already called a number from a chatbot answer and gave out payment or account information, contact your bank or card issuer immediately to dispute charges and freeze the account
reports.howItWorks: Researchers at Vigilance Security identified a campaign they call "Dark Sourcery" in which attackers borrow search engine optimization techniques, but apply them to AI answer engines instead. They mass-produce content such as fake forum posts, PDFs, reviews, and support pages seeded with fraudulent phone numbers, email addresses, and login pages, designed to be picked up and repeated by AI assistants when users ask "what is the customer support number for [company]." When a victim asks a chatbot for a company's support line, refund department, account recovery help, or software download link, the AI may confidently present the attacker's fabricated contact information as fact, without the user ever visiting the poisoned page that supplied it. Victims who call the fake number or visit the fake login page are then asked for credit card numbers, bank login credentials, or other payment details by someone posing as legitimate company support staff.
redFlags: A phone number or contact link for a well-known company was provided by an AI chatbot or AI search summary rather than the company's own verified website
The 'support agent' who answers immediately asks for a credit card number, full bank login, or payment card data to 'fix' an account, refund, or booking
The support contact info surfaced by the AI cannot be found on the official company website or app when checked directly
Unsolicited offers to help move a flight, unlock a bank account, or process a refund come from a number obtained via a chatbot search rather than a number you looked up yourself
realExamples: Vigilance Security researchers counted tens of thousands of malicious pages seeded with fake support numbers, email addresses, login pages, and software-update instructions, affecting at least 374 companies including Fortune 100 firms, airlines, banks, travel companies, and software providers.
Named brands caught up in the campaign reportedly included Delta, Lufthansa, Qatar Airways, Chase, Bank of America, Airbnb, and TripAdvisor.

Vigilance told Dark Reading it had seen a few occurrences of people complaining about being scammed into giving up payment card details after a chatbot-provided phone number connected them to someone who offered to help move a flight or unlock a bank account before asking for credit card details.
reports.source: Dark Reading, https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/attackers-manipulate-ai-chatbots-mass-disinformation-phishing-campaign
spreadPlatforms: Google AI Overview / AI Search Results

reports.title: Parcel Mule / "Parcel Expert" Reshipping Job Scam
reports.summary: Scammers recruit people via unsolicited messages for a fake work-from-home "Parcel Expert" job that actually involves receiving, repackaging, and reshipping merchandise bought with stolen credit cards, turning victims into unwitting mules for stolen goods.
safetyTips: Never accept a job that requires you to receive and reship packages from your home address, especially if contacted out of the blue
Research the hiring company independently and search for complaints or scam reports rather than relying on links sent by a recruiter
Never give copies of your ID, banking information, or other sensitive documents to an online 'employer' before any formal, verifiable hiring process
Be suspicious of any job that promises high income for minimal, vague logistics work with flexible hours
Do not interact with the scammer, do not forward any packages you did not personally order, and report the incident to the proper authorities (in the US, the FTC)
reports.howItWorks: Targets are contacted out of the blue by email, social media DM, or WhatsApp with a job offer from someone claiming to work in a "Logistics Department" for a well-known retailer or shipping company. The message offers a flexible, high-paying remote role — titled something like "Parcel Expert" — where the victim's only duties are to receive packages at their home address, check the items against invoices, take photos, repackage them, and forward them to a "distribution hub," sometimes internationally. In reality, the packages contain merchandise purchased with stolen payment card information, and the victim is unknowingly helping criminals launder stolen goods by breaking the shipping trail. Victims are often asked to hand over personal documents and banking details during a fake "onboarding" process, and are never actually paid for the "work."
redFlags: Unsolicited job offer for well-paid remote work received, inspecting, and reshipping packages
Legitimate companies do not ship high-value goods to a private home address of someone they just hired online
Job offer invokes trusted big-name retailers or carriers (Amazon, FedEx, Walmart, Best Buy, DHL, AliExpress, Zappos) as a trust signal
High pay for low-skill, home-based work with flexible hours and no interview
Requests to send packages onward to another address, hub, or international destination
Requests for personal ID documents or banking details during onboarding
realExamples: Malwarebytes documented a message reading in part: "My name is Elena from the Logistics Department. We reviewed your profile and would like to offer you a position as a Parcel Expert" promising a remote part-time role paying up to $5,300 a month for receiving, checking, and forwarding packages.

Malwarebytes found the companies named in these offers vary by region: a German target was recruited to work for DHL, a Spanish target received an offer for 'mercado,' and a US target got an offer referencing a company called Freight Metro, with Amazon, FedEx, Best Buy, AliExpress, and Walmart also commonly invoked.
reports.source: Malwarebytes, https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/scams/2026/06/beware-of-parcel-expert-job-offers-theyre-parcel-mule-scams

reports.title: Fake TikTok "Rewards" / Loyalty App Scam
reports.summary: Scam websites dressed up as TikTok "rewards" or loyalty programs promise users cash for daily check-ins, referrals, and simple tasks, but the growing balance is fake and can never actually be withdrawn.
relatedScams: TikTok "VIP Upgrade" Crypto Inheritance DM Scam
Fake Retail Coupon / Promo Code Scam
safetyTips: Remember TikTok's real Creator Rewards Program is only for eligible creators who meet specific platform requirements, not for check-ins or tasks on a separate website
Don't assume a rewards site is legitimate just because it carries a TikTok logo or welcome message
Never download a third-party app or hand over banking/personal details just to 'verify' a withdrawal
Treat growing on-screen balances and countdown timers as manipulation tactics, not real money, since the numbers are generated by the site itself with no connection to TikTok's systems
reports.howItWorks: Victims land on a site or app built to look like a mobile shopping or loyalty program, complete with a TikTok logo, a "welcome back" greeting, a daily check-in tracker, and tabs for tasks, referrals, and a profile. Completing check-ins and tasks earns "points" that convert into a cash balance that can look like thousands of dollars, often paired with a countdown timer warning that the balance is about to expire to pressure quick action. When the user tries to redeem the low minimum withdrawal, the site always introduces one more requirement before cashing out — refer more friends, watch more videos, complete a sponsored offer through an affiliate network, or download a separate app to "verify" identity. None of the numbers reflect a real ledger; the balance, points, and countdown are simply invented by the site operator, who actually profits through affiliate and cost-per-action payouts or by getting victims to install adware-laden apps.
redFlags: A site or app uses TikTok branding to offer large cash rewards for daily check-ins, referrals, or simple tasks separate from TikTok's own platform
A countdown timer claims your balance will expire if you don't act immediately
Every time you get close to withdrawing, a new requirement appears (refer more people, watch more videos, complete an offer, download an app)
The promised cash balance or points total seems unrealistically large for the small amount of effort involved
realExamples: Malwarebytes documented TikTok-branded rewards pages built to look like a mobile shopping or loyalty app, with a daily check-in tracker and tabs for tasks, referrals, and profile, where users were told to refer more friends, watch more videos, complete a sponsored offer, or download an app before they could withdraw their 'earnings.'
reports.source: Malwarebytes, https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/scams/2026/08/fake-tiktok-rewards-promise-cash-youll-never-get

reports.title: Tap-to-Pay Charity Donation Scam
reports.summary: Fake fundraisers approach people in public with a phone and ask for a small tap-to-pay donation, but secretly key in a vastly larger amount before the victim taps, turning an intended $15-$20 gift into a charge of thousands of dollars.
safetyTips: Avoid using tap-to-pay features to make donations, or at a minimum, review the details of the transaction before you tap your payment method
Always do your research before giving to a charity

Visit the secretary of state's charities search page to determine if a charity is registered, or check third-party rating companies like the Better Business Bureau's give.org, CharityWatch, or Charity Navigator
Review your financial statements after making an in-person donation to check for charges larger than you authorized
If you believe you've been a victim of a charity scam, file a complaint with the attorney general's office
reports.howItWorks: A solicitor — often young and well-dressed, claiming to represent a charity and sometimes offering music CDs in exchange for donations — approaches someone in a public place like a waterfront area and asks for a small donation. When the target agrees to give something like $15 or $20, the solicitor offers to accept the donation using the tap-to-pay feature on their phone. The donor agrees but does not review the transaction details before tapping. Instead of entering the small amount the donor agreed to, the solicitor secretly enters a far larger figure into the device. The victim doesn't realize what happened until they review their financial statements at a later date and discover a charge much larger than they authorized. In at least one documented case the "charity" involved was actually a for-profit LLC that was not registered as a charitable organization with the state or listed with the IRS as a public charity.
redFlags: A stranger soliciting donations in a public place asks to accept the donation via tap-to-pay on their own phone rather than cash or a verifiable method
You are asked to tap your payment method without being shown or reviewing the transaction details before tapping
The "charity" can't be independently verified as registered with the secretary of state's charities search page or listed with the IRS as a public charity
Solicitors cluster in busy public areas like a waterfront and solicit modest donations in person
realExamples: The Washington State Attorney General's Office received multiple reports during the 2024 holiday season of young, well-dressed men soliciting near the Seattle waterfront claiming to collect donations for a charity called the Youth Upliftment Society, which was organized as a for-profit LLC and was not registered as a charitable organization with the Washington Secretary of State or listed with the IRS as a public charity. In one example, a donor agreed to give $15 but later identified a charge for $4,800; in another, a donor agreed to give $20 and later found a charge of nearly $5,000.
reports.source: Washington State Attorney General's Office, https://www.atg.wa.gov/news/news-releases/consumer-alert-watch-out-potential-scam-charities-requesting-donations-tap-pay

reports.title: Search Parameter Injection Fake Support Number Scam
reports.summary: Scammers buy sponsored Google ads that use malicious URL parameters to inject a fake "customer support" phone number directly into the real, legitimate website of brands like Netflix, Apple, Microsoft, and Bank of America. Because the page is 100% authentic and the address bar shows the real domain, victims have no reason to suspect the number is fraudulent.
relatedScams: SEO Poisoning Bank Account Takeover Scam
safetyTips: Never trust a phone number that appears after clicking a sponsored search ad — navigate to support pages directly through the company's app or by typing the known official URL
Verify any customer service number against the back of your card, a billing statement, or the company's official app before calling
Use a browser security extension capable of detecting search/URL hijacking attempts
Never give remote access to your device or share one-time codes/passwords with anyone who called or whom you reached via a number found in search results
If you already called a suspicious number, change your passwords and monitor financial accounts immediately
reports.howItWorks: A person searches Google for a company's customer service number and clicks a sponsored ad that actually leads to the genuine brand website. However, the ad's URL contains crafted search-query parameters that exploit a "reflected input vulnerability" — the site's own search function blindly displays whatever text is fed into that parameter without sanitizing it. This lets scammers make their own phone number appear prominently inside what looks like an official search result or support section on the real page. The browser address bar shows the legitimate domain, so there's no obvious red flag. When the victim calls the number believing it's the company's real help line, scammers posing as support agents ask for login credentials, financial account details, or remote access to the victim's device under the guise of resolving an account issue.
redFlags: A phone number embedded directly in a long, odd-looking URL with lots of encoded characters
The support number appears inside a search results box on the page rather than in the company's normal official contact page
You reached the page by clicking a sponsored/ad link from a search engine rather than typing the company's URL or using its app
The phone agent immediately asks for passwords, account credentials, or remote-access software installation
The displayed number differs from the number listed in the company's official app or billing statements
realExamples: Malwarebytes identified fake support numbers inserted into real pages for Apple, Bank of America, Facebook, HP, Microsoft, Netflix, and PayPal via sponsored search ads using malicious URL parameters.

Researchers found Netflix's own search function would blindly reflect whatever text was placed in its query parameter without sanitization, letting scammers display their number as if it were an official result.
Malwarebytes' Browser Guard displayed a 'Search Hijacking Detected' warning after flagging the unauthorized number insertions on these hijacked but genuine pages.
reports.source: Malwarebytes, https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2025/06/scammers-hijack-websites-of-bank-of-america-netflix-microsoft-and-more-to-insert-fake-phone-number
